\textbf{\textcolor{red}{9. Worked Example 2 --- RW + noise, dynamic state ($W > 0$)}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{WORKED EXAMPLE --- RW + noise (DYNAMIC state, $W > 0$).}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Setup.}} Full local-level state-space model, state \emph{not} fixed (random walk with non-zero variance):

$\bullet$ \emph{State equation (random walk):} $\;\theta_t \;=\; \theta_{t-1} + w_t,\qquad w_t \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0,\, W),\quad W > 0,$ with $\theta_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(m_0,\, C_0)$.

$\bullet$ \emph{Observation equation:} $\;Y_t \;=\; \theta_t + \varepsilon_t,\qquad \varepsilon_t \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0,\, V),\quad \{\varepsilon_t\} \perp \{w_t\} \perp \theta_0.$

\emph{DLM tuple (specialisation of the general template):} $\;G = 1,\;\; F = 1,\;\; W = W,\;\; V = V.$ State is 1D; everything stays scalar.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Suppose we have already filtered up to time $T$.}} After processing $y_{1:T}$, the filter outputs the current state posterior
\[ \theta_T \mid y_{1:T} \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(m_T,\, C_T). \]
Now run the two-step Gaussian-simplification recipe to forecast $\theta_{T+1}$ and $Y_{T+1}$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Step 1 --- Predict the state $f(\theta_{T+1} \mid y_{1:T})$.}}

Push the filtered posterior through the transition. Generic formula: $a_{T+1} = G\, m_T$, $R_{T+1} = G\, C_T\, G^\top + W$. With $G = 1$ this collapses to
\[ \boxed{\; \theta_{T+1} \mid y_{1:T} \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(a_{T+1},\, R_{T+1}), \qquad a_{T+1} \;=\; m_T, \qquad R_{T+1} \;=\; C_T + W. \;} \]

\emph{Reading.} The predicted mean is just $m_T$ (RW has no drift). The predicted variance is the filtered variance \emph{plus} a fresh chunk $W$ injected by the transition: even if you knew $\theta_T$ exactly, $\theta_{T+1}$ would still wander by $\mathcal{N}(0, W)$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Step 2 --- Predict the observation $f(Y_{T+1} \mid y_{1:T})$.}}

Push the predicted state through the emission. Generic formula: $f_{T+1} = F\, a_{T+1}$, $Q_{T+1} = F\, R_{T+1}\, F^\top + V$. With $F = 1$, $V = V$:
\[ \boxed{\; Y_{T+1} \mid y_{1:T} \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(f_{T+1},\, Q_{T+1}), \qquad f_{T+1} \;=\; m_T, \qquad Q_{T+1} \;=\; C_T + W + V. \;} \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Three sources of forecast uncertainty in $Q_{T+1}$.}} Read off the decomposition:
\[ Q_{T+1} \;=\; \underbrace{C_T}_{\substack{\text{(1) state posterior} \\ \text{uncertainty (carried)}}} \;+\; \underbrace{W}_{\substack{\text{(2) new state innovation} \\ \text{(only present if } W > 0)}} \;+\; \underbrace{V}_{\substack{\text{(3) observation} \\ \text{noise}}}. \]

$\bullet$ \emph{(1) $C_T$ --- posterior uncertainty about the current state.} After all $T$ filtering steps, we still don't know $\theta_T$ exactly --- this is the residual variance from filtering. Carried forward unchanged because $G = 1$.

$\bullet$ \emph{(2) $W$ --- new state innovation.} The walk's own randomness between $T$ and $T+1$: even knowing $\theta_T$ exactly, the next state is $\theta_T + w_{T+1}$, $w_{T+1} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, W)$. \textbf{This term is the new entry compared to the fixed-state case.}

$\bullet$ \emph{(3) $V$ --- observation noise.} The measurement noise on $Y_{T+1}$, unavoidable even if you knew $\theta_{T+1}$ exactly.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Fixed-state special case ($W = 0$) recovers the previous worked example.}}

Setting $W = 0$ kills term (2):
\[ a_{T+1} = m_T, \qquad R_{T+1} = C_T, \qquad f_{T+1} = m_T, \qquad Q_{T+1} = C_T + V. \]
Identical to the fixed-state worked example: the state can't change, so the only sources of forecast variance are filter residual uncertainty $C_T$ and observation noise $V$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Full filter recursion at time $T+1$.}} For completeness: once $y_{T+1}$ arrives, apply the Kalman update with $R_{T+1}$ as the predicted-prior variance:

\emph{Predict (above):} $a_{T+1} = m_T,\quad R_{T+1} = C_T + W$.

\emph{Update:} blend predicted prior with new datum.
\[ \frac{1}{C_{T+1}} \;=\; \frac{1}{R_{T+1}} + \frac{1}{V}, \qquad m_{T+1} \;=\; C_{T+1}\Bigl(\tfrac{a_{T+1}}{R_{T+1}} + \tfrac{y_{T+1}}{V}\Bigr). \]

\emph{Kalman gain form (equivalent):}
\[ m_{T+1} \;=\; a_{T+1} + K_{T+1}\, \underbrace{(y_{T+1} - f_{T+1})}_{e_{T+1}\,=\,\text{innovation}}, \qquad K_{T+1} \;=\; \frac{R_{T+1}}{R_{T+1} + V} \;=\; \frac{C_T + W}{C_T + W + V}. \]
$K_{T+1} \to 1$ when the state is much more uncertain than the observation noise (trust the new datum); $K_{T+1} \to 0$ in the opposite regime.

\emph{Signal-to-noise ratio.} The book (Petris--Petrone--Campagnoli, p.\ 39) names $W / V$ as the SNR: it is the single dimensionless number controlling how reactive the filter is. High SNR $\Rightarrow K \to 1$ (filter tracks every wiggle); low SNR $\Rightarrow K \to 0$ (filter smooths heavily, treating data as noise around an essentially-constant state).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{$h$-step forecast.}} Iterate Step 1 forward $h$ times. With $G = 1$: $a_{T+h} = m_T$ for all $h$, and $R_{T+h} = C_T + h\, W$ (each step adds $W$). Then $Q_{T+h} = R_{T+h} + V = C_T + h W + V$:
\[ \boxed{\; Y_{T+h} \mid y_{1:T} \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(m_T,\; C_T + h\, W + V). \;} \]
Forecast bands fan out linearly in $h$ --- the hallmark of a random-walk signal.

\emph{Kalman gain form (equivalent):}
\[ m_{T+1} \;=\; a_{T+1} + K_{T+1}\, \underbrace{(y_{T+1} - f_{T+1})}_{e_{T+1}\,=\,\text{innovation}}, \qquad K_{T+1} \;=\; \frac{R_{T+1}}{R_{T+1} + V} \;=\; \frac{C_T + W}{C_T + W + V}. \]
$K_{T+1} \to 1$ when the state is much more uncertain than the observation noise (trust the new datum); $K_{T+1} \to 0$ in the opposite regime.

\emph{Signal-to-noise ratio.} The book (Petris--Petrone--Campagnoli, p.\ 39) names $W / V$ as the SNR: it is the single dimensionless number controlling how reactive the filter is. High SNR $\Rightarrow K \to 1$ (filter tracks every wiggle); low SNR $\Rightarrow K \to 0$ (filter smooths heavily, treating data as noise around an essentially-constant state).


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Prediction-error correction (Kalman) form.}} Algebraically simplifying the precision-blend formula for $m_n$ (recursive column) gives the interpretable Kalman update
\[ \boxed{\; m_n \;=\; m_{n-1} + K_n\, \underbrace{(y_n - m_{n-1})}_{e_n \,=\, \text{prediction error}}, \qquad K_n \;=\; \frac{C_{n-1}}{C_{n-1} + \sigma^2}. \;} \]
$e_n = y_n - m_{n-1}$ is the innovation. $K_n$ goes up (we trust the new observation more) when reliability is high.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Two readings of the Kalman gain $K_n$.}}

$\bullet$ \textbf{(1) Ratio of variances (signal-to-total).} Of the total variability of $Y_n$, what fraction comes from \emph{state uncertainty} (informative about $\theta_n$) vs \emph{observation noise} (uninformative)? State dominates $\Rightarrow K_n \to 1$; noise dominates $\Rightarrow K_n \to 0$.

trash.title: Global trend (linear) --- fixed drift with iid noise
trash.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{GLOBAL TREND --- linear trend with iid noise (textbook deterministic-trend DLM).}}

The book (Petris-Petrone-Campagnoli, p.\ 117 and Problem 3.8 p.\ 130) calls this the \textbf{global trend model}. Same mean as RW + drift but errors are \emph{iid}, not accumulating.

\begin{keydef}
\textbf{Global (deterministic) linear trend.}
\[ Y_t \;=\; \mu_0 + \delta\, t + \varepsilon_t, \qquad \varepsilon_t \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0,\, \sigma^2), \qquad t = 1, 2, \dots \]
Parameters: $\mu_0$ (initial level), $\delta$ (global slope $=$ \emph{fixed drift}); $\sigma^2$ obs-noise variance.
\end{keydef}

\emph{As a degenerate DLM.} State $\theta_t = (\mu_0,\, \delta)^\top$ frozen forever; the time-dependence is pushed into a time-varying $F_t$:
\[ \theta_t = \theta_{t-1} \quad (W = 0), \qquad Y_t = F_t\, \theta_t + \varepsilon_t \quad \text{with}\ F_t = (1,\; t),\ V = \sigma^2. \]
i.e.\ $G = I_2$, $F_t = (1,\, t)$, $W = 0$, $V = \sigma^2$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Relation to other models.}}

$\bullet$ \emph{vs.\ RW + drift (Example 2B).} Same mean function $E[Y_t] = \mu_0 + \delta t$ in both. The difference is in the \textbf{error structure}, not the trend.

$\quad\bullet$ \emph{Global trend:} only obs noise $\varepsilon_t$ (iid). $\mathrm{Var}(Y_t) = \sigma^2$, constant. No memory --- $Y_t$ values are conditionally independent given $(\mu_0, \delta)$.

$\quad\bullet$ \emph{RW + drift:} adds an accumulating state-noise $w_t$ (random walk on top of the trend). $\mathrm{Var}(Y_t) = t\, \sigma_w^2 + \sigma_\varepsilon^2$, grows linearly. Full memory --- past shocks live in the level forever.

$\quad\bullet$ Both are non-stationary in mean; only global trend has constant variance.

$\bullet$ \emph{vs.\ LLT (Example 5).} LLT generalises by letting the slope wander: $\beta_t = \beta_{t-1} + w_{2,t}$. Global trend is the LLT special case with \textbf{both} state-noise variances zero, $\sigma_{w_1}^2 = \sigma_{w_2}^2 = 0$ (see DLMwR p.\ 117, after eq.\ 3.35):
\[ \text{LLT}\;\xrightarrow{\sigma_{w_1}^2 = 0,\ \sigma_{w_2}^2 = 0}\;\text{Global trend}. \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Hierarchy of trend DLMs.}}
\[ \boxed{\;\text{Global trend} \;\subset\; \text{RW + drift} \;\subset\; \text{LLT}.\;} \]

$\bullet$ \emph{Global trend:} $W = 0$, fixed slope --- simplest, deterministic state.

$\bullet$ \emph{RW + drift:} $\sigma_{w_1}^2 > 0$ (level wanders) but $\sigma_{w_2}^2 = 0$ (slope fixed).

$\bullet$ \emph{LLT:} both noises non-zero (level and slope both wander).

\emph{One-line takeaway.} The \emph{drift} is the same constant slope in all three. What changes is the noise around it: iid (global trend) $\to$ integrated (RW + drift) $\to$ doubly-integrated (LLT).

trash.title: Example 5: Local Linear Trend (LLT)
Example 7: Dynamic Linear Regression (DLR)
trash.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{EXAMPLE 7 --- Dynamic Linear Regression (DLR).}}

A regression of $Y_t$ on a covariate $x_t$ where the regression \emph{coefficients themselves vary over time} (typically each as a random walk). The regressor enters via a \emph{time-varying observation matrix} $F_t$, not via fixed parameters.

\begin{keydef}
\textbf{Dynamic Linear Regression (DLR) DLM.}

\emph{State} $\theta_t = (\alpha_t,\, \beta_t)^\top \in \mathbb{R}^2$ (time-varying intercept $\alpha_t$ and slope $\beta_t$).

\emph{State equations (random-walk coefficients).}
\[ \alpha_t \;=\; \alpha_{t-1} + w_{1,t}, \qquad w_{1,t} \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0,\, \sigma_{w_1}^2); \]
\[ \beta_t \;=\; \beta_{t-1} + w_{2,t}, \qquad w_{2,t} \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0,\, \sigma_{w_2}^2). \]
In matrix form:
\[ \theta_t \;=\; \underbrace{I_2}_{G}\, \theta_{t-1} + w_t, \qquad w_t = (w_{1,t},\, w_{2,t})^\top \sim \mathcal{N}_2\!\bigl(0,\; W\bigr), \quad W = \mathrm{diag}(\sigma_{w_1}^2,\, \sigma_{w_2}^2). \]

\emph{Observation equation (regression with time-varying coefficient).}
\[ Y_t \;=\; \alpha_t + \beta_t\, x_t + v_t \;=\; \underbrace{(1,\; x_t)}_{F_t}\, \theta_t + v_t, \qquad v_t \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0,\, \sigma^2). \]

All noises $\{w_t\}, \{v_t\}$ and the initial state $\theta_0 \sim \mathcal{N}_2(m_0, C_0)$ mutually independent.
\end{keydef}

\emph{Where the regressor lives.} The covariate $x_t$ enters \textbf{$F_t$} (the observation matrix), not the state. The \emph{state} is the coefficients $(\alpha_t, \beta_t)$. Each new $t$ brings a new $F_t = (1, x_t)$ that combines the known regressor value with the unknown coefficients.

\emph{DLM tuple (time-varying $F_t$).}
\[ G = I_2, \qquad F_t = (1,\; x_t), \qquad W = \mathrm{diag}(\sigma_{w_1}^2,\, \sigma_{w_2}^2), \qquad V = \sigma^2. \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Special cases.}}

$\bullet$ \emph{Static regression} (classical OLS setup): $\sigma_{w_1}^2 = \sigma_{w_2}^2 = 0$ (no state noise) $\Rightarrow$ $\alpha_t \equiv \alpha_0$, $\beta_t \equiv \beta_0$ fixed forever. The DLM collapses to ordinary linear regression $Y_t = \alpha_0 + \beta_0 x_t + v_t$ with $\alpha_0, \beta_0$ jointly estimated from the data via Bayes (closed form for $V$ known).

$\bullet$ \emph{Only the intercept drifts:} $\sigma_{w_2}^2 = 0$ $\Rightarrow$ a regression with a wandering level and a fixed slope.

$\bullet$ \emph{Only the slope drifts:} $\sigma_{w_1}^2 = 0$ $\Rightarrow$ regression with constant intercept and time-varying sensitivity to $x_t$ (e.g.\ time-varying $\beta$ of a stock against the market).

$\bullet$ \emph{Local linear trend (Example 5) is a special case of DLR:} take $x_t = t$ (the regressor is just time itself). Then $Y_t = \alpha_t + \beta_t \cdot t + v_t$ with both coefficients drifting --- same as LLT's level + slope structure (after a re-parametrisation).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Multiple regressors.}} Extends trivially: state $\theta_t = (\alpha_t, \beta_{1,t}, \dots, \beta_{k,t})^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{k+1}$, observation matrix $F_t = (1, x_{1,t}, \dots, x_{k,t})$, $G = I_{k+1}$, $W = \mathrm{diag}(\sigma_{w_0}^2, \sigma_{w_1}^2, \dots, \sigma_{w_k}^2)$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Why useful.}}

$\bullet$ \emph{Time-varying betas} in finance: the sensitivity of a stock to the market index changes over the business cycle.

$\bullet$ \emph{Marketing-mix models:} the effectiveness of advertising spend varies seasonally or by phase of product life-cycle.

$\bullet$ \emph{Macroeconomic relationships:} elasticities (e.g.\ consumption-income, Phillips curve slope) drift over decades.

$\bullet$ \emph{Clinical-trial models:} patient covariates can have time-varying effects (e.g.\ drug efficacy that decays).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Past-exam note.}} The May 2024 Q4 question ("clinical-trial covariate DLM") is a DLR. The standard answer is to (i) write the model in DLM form with regressor in $F_t$, (ii) run the Kalman filter on the state $\theta_t = (\alpha_t, \beta_t)^\top$, (iii) report posterior means and uncertainties.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Estimation.}} Same Kalman recursion as any DLM --- only difference is that $F_t$ changes each period:
\[ a_t = G\, m_{t-1} = m_{t-1};\quad R_t = C_{t-1} + W;\quad f_t = F_t\, a_t = a_t^{\alpha} + x_t\, a_t^{\beta};\quad Q_t = F_t\, R_t\, F_t^\top + V;\quad K_t = R_t F_t^\top Q_t^{-1};\quad m_t = a_t + K_t(y_t - f_t);\quad C_t = R_t - K_t F_t R_t. \]
Notice that $K_t$ is now a \emph{column vector} (size $2 \times 1$) because $F_t$ is $1 \times 2$ --- the Kalman gain tells you how to update each coefficient given the surprise.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Book reference.}} Petris-Petrone-Campagnoli, Section 3.2.4 "Dynamic linear regression models", pp. 104--108.

trash.title: LLT: prior, filtered posterior, marginal of mu_t
trash.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{LLT --- initial state, filtered posterior, marginal of $\mu_t$.}}

Companion to Example 5 (LLT). Spells out the joint Gaussian prior on $\theta_0$, the joint filtered posterior $\theta_t \mid y_{1:t}$, and how to extract the marginal posterior of just the \emph{level} $\mu_t$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Initial state (prior).}} Two-component state, two-component prior moments:
\[ \theta_0 \;=\; (\mu_0,\, \beta_0)^\top \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}_2\!\bigl(m_0,\; C_0\bigr), \qquad m_0 \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} m_0^{\mu} \\ m_0^{\beta} \end{pmatrix}, \qquad C_0 \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} C_0^{\mu\mu} & C_0^{\mu\beta} \\ C_0^{\mu\beta} & C_0^{\beta\beta} \end{pmatrix}. \]
$\bullet$ $m_0^{\mu}$ = prior mean of the level $\mu_0$.

$\bullet$ $m_0^{\beta}$ = prior mean of the slope $\beta_0$.

$\bullet$ $C_0^{\mu\mu}$ = prior variance of the level.

$\bullet$ $C_0^{\beta\beta}$ = prior variance of the slope.

$\bullet$ $C_0^{\mu\beta}$ = prior covariance between level and slope.

A common default is $C_0$ diagonal (no a-priori correlation between level and slope) and a relatively large $C_0^{\mu\mu}, C_0^{\beta\beta}$ ("diffuse" prior).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Filtered posterior at time $t$.}} After observing $y_{1:t}$, the Kalman filter gives a 2D Gaussian posterior:
\[ \theta_t \mid y_{1:t} \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} \mu_t \\ \beta_t \end{pmatrix} \Big| y_{1:t} \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}_2\!\bigl(m_t,\; C_t\bigr), \qquad m_t \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} m_t^{\mu} \\ m_t^{\beta} \end{pmatrix}, \qquad C_t \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} C_t^{\mu\mu} & C_t^{\mu\beta} \\ C_t^{\mu\beta} & C_t^{\beta\beta} \end{pmatrix}. \]
Interpretation:

$\bullet$ $m_t^{\mu} = E[\mu_t \mid y_{1:t}]$ --- our best (squared-loss) estimate of the current \emph{level}.

$\bullet$ $m_t^{\beta} = E[\beta_t \mid y_{1:t}]$ --- our best estimate of the current \emph{slope}.

$\bullet$ $C_t^{\mu\mu} = \mathrm{Var}(\mu_t \mid y_{1:t})$ --- posterior \emph{variance} of the level (how uncertain we are about $\mu_t$).

$\bullet$ $C_t^{\beta\beta} = \mathrm{Var}(\beta_t \mid y_{1:t})$ --- posterior \emph{variance} of the slope.

$\bullet$ $C_t^{\mu\beta} = \mathrm{Cov}(\mu_t,\, \beta_t \mid y_{1:t})$ --- their posterior \emph{covariance} (typically non-zero even if $C_0$ was diagonal: filtering through $G = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ creates correlations).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Marginal posterior of $\mu_t$ alone.}} If you only care about the level $\mu_t$ (ignoring uncertainty about the slope), \textbf{integrate $\beta_t$ out of the joint}:
\[ f(\mu_t \mid y_{1:t}) \;=\; \int f(\mu_t,\, \beta_t \mid y_{1:t})\, d\beta_t. \]
For a Gaussian joint this is immediate --- the marginal of a Gaussian is Gaussian, with the corresponding component of the mean and the diagonal entry of the covariance:
\[ \boxed{\; \mu_t \mid y_{1:t} \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}\!\bigl(m_t^{\mu},\;\; C_t^{\mu\mu}\bigr). \;} \]
That is: just \emph{read off} the first entry of $m_t$ and the $(1,1)$ entry of $C_t$. (Same trick for the slope alone: $\beta_t \mid y_{1:t} \sim \mathcal{N}(m_t^{\beta},\, C_t^{\beta\beta})$.)

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Why $C_t^{\mu\mu}$, not the full $C_t$, for forecasting $Y_{t+h}$.}} Recall $Y_{t+h} = F\, \theta_{t+h} + v_{t+h}$ with $F = (1, 0)$. The observation predictive variance is
\[ Q_{t+h} \;=\; F\, R_{t+h}\, F^\top + V \;=\; [R_{t+h}]_{\mu\mu} + \sigma^2, \]
i.e.\ only the level-variance entry of $R_{t+h}$ matters. The slope's variance and the level-slope covariance affect $Q_{t+h}$ only \emph{indirectly} through how they shape $[R_{t+h}]_{\mu\mu}$ as $h$ grows ($\sim h^3$ growth, as derived in the cheatsheet).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Point estimates.}} Under squared loss (the default), the Bayes-optimal point estimates are the marginal means:
\[ \hat\mu_t \;=\; m_t^{\mu}, \qquad \hat\beta_t \;=\; m_t^{\beta}, \qquad \hat Y_{t+h} \;=\; f_{t+h} \;=\; m_t^{\mu} + h\, m_t^{\beta} \quad (\text{evaluated via } G^h m_t \text{ for } G = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)). \]

\emph{Take-away.} The 2D joint posterior is what the filter produces; marginals (for individual point estimates and uncertainty on level alone or slope alone) come from picking out the matching component of the mean and diagonal of the covariance --- no integration needed because Gaussian marginals collapse to the obvious entries.

trash.title: Boh
trash.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{6. Likelihood (for parameter estimation)} $\;\;f(y_{1:T} \mid \phi)$.} \emph{If the model has unknown parameters $\phi$.} Marginalise out the hidden path:
\[ f(y_{1:T} \mid \phi) \;=\; \int f(y_{1:T},\, \theta_{0:T} \mid \phi)\, d\theta_{0:T}. \]
This is the building block for both:

$\bullet$ \emph{Frequentist}: maximise over $\phi$ to get the MLE $\hat\phi$.

$\bullet$ \emph{Bayesian}: combine with a prior $\pi(\phi)$ via Bayes' rule, $f(\phi \mid y_{1:T}) \propto f(y_{1:T} \mid \phi)\, \pi(\phi)$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Putting parameter uncertainty into prediction.}}

$\bullet$ \emph{Frequentist plug-in.} Take $\hat\phi$, then compute $f(y_{T+1} \mid y_{1:T}, \hat\phi)$ by the rules above. \emph{Pretends $\hat\phi$ is the truth} --- forecast bands too narrow.

$\bullet$ \emph{Bayesian posterior predictive.} Integrate out $\phi$:
\[ f(y_{T+1} \mid y_{1:T}) \;=\; \int f(y_{T+1} \mid y_{1:T}, \phi)\, f(\phi \mid y_{1:T})\, d\phi. \]
This is just \emph{Bayes' rule applied twice}: once to get the filtered/predicted state distribution given $\phi$, then again to integrate out the parameter. Forecast bands honestly account for parameter uncertainty.


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Worked example (HMM weather/activity).}} The recursion we used in the filtering exercise,
\[ \alpha_t(j) \;=\; \underbrace{b_{j, y_t}}_{\text{likelihood of new obs}} \;\cdot\; \underbrace{\sum_{i} \alpha_{t-1}(i)\, p_{i,j}}_{\text{prior carried forward}}, \]
is exactly the SSM filtering formula above, with discrete states. The \emph{predict} half (the sum) propagates yesterday's belief through $\mathbf{P}$; the \emph{update} half (the multiplication by $b_{j, y_t}$) is Bayes applied to today's observation.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Bottom line.}} There is only one engine: \emph{posterior $\propto$ likelihood $\cdot$ prior}, with marginalisation to remove unwanted variables. Filtering, smoothing, prediction, decoding, MLE, posterior predictive --- each is just that engine pointed at a different conditional or marginal of the SSM joint.

trash.title: Fixed regression model (cross-sectional, no time)
trash.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{FIXED REGRESSION MODEL (cross-sectional, no time dimension; per-observation slope $\beta_i$).}}

Regression of $Y$ on a covariate $x$ across \emph{individuals} (index $i$, not time). Slope $\beta_i$ is allowed to vary per observation.

\begin{keydef}
\textbf{Cross-sectional regression with individual-specific slope.}
\[ Y_i \;=\; \alpha + \beta_i\, x_i + \varepsilon_i, \qquad \varepsilon_i \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0,\, \sigma^2), \qquad i = 1, \dots, n. \]
$\alpha$ is the common intercept; $\beta_i$ is the slope for observation $i$ (can differ across $i$); $\sigma^2$ is the noise variance. Index $i$ runs over individuals/observations, \emph{not} time.
\end{keydef}

\emph{Identifiability caveat.} With $n$ observations and $n$ unknown slopes, the model is \emph{not identified} without further structure on $\beta_i$. Four standard restrictions, all of which collapse the model back into a single DLM with a static state and a richer $F_i$:

$\bullet$ \emph{Case A --- $\beta_i$ depends on a known covariate $z_i$ (interaction).}
\[ \beta_i = \beta_0 + \gamma\, z_i \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; Y_i = \alpha + \beta_0 x_i + \gamma (z_i x_i) + \varepsilon_i. \]
Effect of $x$ depends linearly on $z$ (e.g., $z =$ age $\Rightarrow$ price elasticity varies with age).

$\bullet$ \emph{Case B --- $\beta_i$ depends on $x_i$ itself (polynomial / non-linear effect).}
\[ \beta_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; Y_i = \alpha + \beta_0 x_i + \beta_1 x_i^2 + \varepsilon_i \quad (\text{quadratic regression}). \]
Slope changes with the level of $x_i$ (diminishing returns if $\beta_1 < 0$).

$\bullet$ \emph{Case C --- $\beta_i$ is group-specific (categorical) --- $K$ slopes total.}
\[ Y_i = \alpha + \beta_{g(i)}\, x_i + \varepsilon_i, \qquad g(i) \in \{1, \dots, K\}. \]
Each group has its own slope; estimated by interaction dummies $\mathbf{1}\{g(i) = k\}\, x_i$ for each group.

$\bullet$ \emph{Case D --- $\beta_i$ is a random effect (hierarchical model).}
\[ \beta_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\bar\beta,\, \tau^2), \quad Y_i \mid \beta_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\alpha + \beta_i x_i,\, \sigma^2). \]
$\beta_i$ are unobserved random draws from a population; estimate $(\bar\beta, \tau^2)$ rather than each $\beta_i$ separately. Posterior gives a \emph{shrunken} $\hat\beta_i$ pulled toward $\bar\beta$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Conditional distribution per $x_i$.}}
\[ Y_i \mid x_i \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(\alpha + \beta_i\, x_i,\; \sigma^2). \]
At each $x_i$ value, the conditional density is Gaussian centered on $\alpha + \beta_i x_i$, width $\sigma$. The plot below visualises this for the homogeneous-slope special case ($\beta_i \equiv \beta$ constant), showing how the conditional mean shifts with $x_i$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{4-step DLM template (degenerate, static state).}}

\emph{(1) State.} $\theta = (\alpha, \beta_0, \dots)^\top \in \mathbb{R}^k$, \emph{frozen} (no time index, no dynamics). The components of $\theta$ are whatever parameters define $\beta_i$ in the case above (Case A: $(\alpha, \beta_0, \gamma)$; Case B: $(\alpha, \beta_0, \beta_1)$; Case C: $(\alpha, \beta_1, \dots, \beta_K)$; Case D: $(\alpha, \bar\beta, \tau^2, \sigma^2)$ at top of a hierarchy).

\emph{(2) Component equations.} All components frozen: $\theta_{j} = \theta_{j}$. No noise.

\emph{(3) Matrix state eq.} $\theta_i = G\, \theta_{i-1} + w_i = I_k \theta_{i-1} + 0 = \theta_{i-1}$ (state never changes across $i$). $G = I_k$, $W = 0$.

\emph{(4) Observation eq.} $Y_i = F_i\, \theta + \varepsilon_i$ with a \emph{case-dependent} $F_i$:
\[ \text{Case A: } F_i = (1, x_i, z_i x_i); \quad \text{Case B: } F_i = (1, x_i, x_i^2); \quad \text{Case C: } F_i = (1, \mathbf{1}\{g(i)=1\}x_i, \dots, \mathbf{1}\{g(i)=K\}x_i); \]
\[ \text{Case D: } F_i = (1, x_i) \text{ plus latent } \beta_i \text{ in the state (hierarchical SSM)}. \]
$\varepsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Vs.\ Dynamic Linear Regression (DLR, Example 7).}}

$\bullet$ \emph{Fixed regression (this):} coefficients vary \emph{across individuals} $i$ but not across time; state frozen.

$\bullet$ \emph{DLR:} coefficients vary \emph{over time} $t$ (random walks); state evolves; same $F_t = (1, x_t)$ shape.

\emph{Bridge.} DLR is the time-domain analog of Case D of fixed regression: $\beta_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\bar\beta, \tau^2)$ iid across individuals becomes $\beta_t$ random walk across time. Both relax "$\beta$ same everywhere" along different axes (cross-section vs time).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Estimation.}} Cases A--C are standard OLS / MLE: stack the appropriate columns of $F_i$ as a design matrix and regress. Case D needs hierarchical Bayes / mixed-effects (\verb|lmer| in R, \verb|brms| or \verb|stan|).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Why include this in the SSM family map?}} The most degenerate DLM: no time, no dynamics, no state noise --- just a static parameter vector with a per-observation observation matrix $F_i$. Serves as the \emph{baseline} that the dynamic models (LLT / Local linear growth, DLR, etc.) generalise. Plot below visualises the conditional distribution that defines this model.

trash.title: Example 4: AR(2) and AR(p) via state augmentation
trash.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{EXAMPLE 4 --- AR($p$) via state augmentation (book-faithful form, DLMwR pp.\ 112--113).}}

See the \emph{Example SSMs hub} for the canonical DLM template and the worked 2$\times$2 matrix example.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Book convention.}} DLMwR uses an auxiliary-component augmentation (eqs.\ 3.23--3.25), \emph{not} the naive "stack lagged $Y$" form. The book explicitly notes (p.\ 113) that "$F_t$ of a DLM cannot depend on past values of the observations," ruling out lagged-$Y$ as state components.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{First: the AR(2) special case ($p = 2$).}}

\emph{Model.} $Y_t = \phi_1 Y_{t-1} + \phi_2 Y_{t-2} + \varepsilon_t$, $\varepsilon_t \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$.

\emph{(1) State.} $\theta_t = (\theta_{1,t},\, \theta_{2,t})^\top \in \mathbb{R}^2$ with $\theta_{1,t} = Y_t$; $\theta_{2,t}$ is an auxiliary component (not equal to a lagged $Y$ directly).

\emph{(2) Component equations.}
\[ \theta_{1,t} = \phi_1\, \theta_{1,t-1} + \theta_{2,t-1} + \varepsilon_t, \qquad \theta_{2,t} = \phi_2\, \theta_{1,t-1}. \]

\emph{(3) Matrix state eq.}
\[ \begin{pmatrix} \theta_{1,t} \\ \theta_{2,t} \end{pmatrix} \;=\; \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} \phi_1 & 1 \\ \phi_2 & 0 \end{pmatrix}}_{G} \begin{pmatrix} \theta_{1,t-1} \\ \theta_{2,t-1} \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} \varepsilon_t \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad W = \begin{pmatrix} \sigma^2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. \]

\emph{(4) Obs eq.} $Y_t = F\, \theta_t = (1,\, 0)\, \theta_t = \theta_{1,t}$ (degenerate: $V = 0$).

\emph{Verification --- recover the AR(2) recursion.} From the first component equation:
\[ Y_t = \theta_{1,t} = \phi_1 Y_{t-1} + \theta_{2,t-1} + \varepsilon_t. \]
But from the second component (one step back): $\theta_{2,t-1} = \phi_2\, \theta_{1,t-2} = \phi_2 Y_{t-2}$. Substitute:
\[ Y_t = \phi_1 Y_{t-1} + \phi_2 Y_{t-2} + \varepsilon_t. \;\checkmark \]
The auxiliary state $\theta_{2,t}$ acts as a "delayed echo" $\phi_2 Y_{t-1}$ that arrives at the next step.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{General AR($p$) --- 4-step DLM template (book companion form).}}

\emph{(1) State.} $\theta_t = (\theta_{1,t},\, \dots,\, \theta_{p,t})^\top \in \mathbb{R}^p$, with $\theta_{1,t} = Y_t$; $\theta_{2,t}, \dots, \theta_{p,t}$ are auxiliary components (delayed echoes, \emph{not} lagged observations).

\emph{(2) Component equations.}
\[ \theta_{1,t} = \phi_1\, \theta_{1,t-1} + \theta_{2,t-1} + \varepsilon_t, \quad \theta_{j,t} = \phi_j\, \theta_{1,t-1} + \theta_{j+1,t-1} \;\text{ for } j = 2, \dots, p-1, \quad \theta_{p,t} = \phi_p\, \theta_{1,t-1}, \]
with $\varepsilon_t \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$.

\emph{(3) Matrix state equation.}
\[ \begin{pmatrix} \theta_{1,t} \\ \theta_{2,t} \\ \vdots \\ \theta_{p-1,t} \\ \theta_{p,t} \end{pmatrix} \;=\; \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} \phi_1 & 1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ \phi_2 & 0 & 1 & \cdots & 0 \\ \vdots & & & \ddots & \\ \phi_{p-1} & 0 & \cdots & 0 & 1 \\ \phi_p & 0 & \cdots & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}}_{G} \begin{pmatrix} \theta_{1,t-1} \\ \theta_{2,t-1} \\ \vdots \\ \theta_{p-1,t-1} \\ \theta_{p,t-1} \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} \varepsilon_t \\ 0 \\ \vdots \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad W = \mathrm{diag}(\sigma^2,\, 0,\, \dots,\, 0). \]

\emph{(4) Observation equation.} $Y_t = F\, \theta_t + v_t = (1, 0, \dots, 0)\, \theta_t = \theta_{1,t}$, $F = (1, 0, \dots, 0)$, $V = 0$ (degenerate --- state observed exactly).

\emph{Reading.} The $\phi$'s sit in the \emph{first column} of $G$ (not the first row). The super-diagonal of 1's "shifts" auxiliary components, so each $\theta_{j,t-1}$ becomes a delayed contribution to $\theta_{1,\cdot}$ at the next step.

\emph{Why not lagged-$Y$ form?} Many textbooks use the "naive" companion $G$ with $\phi$'s in the first row and $\theta_t = (Y_t, Y_{t-1}, \dots, Y_{t-p+1})^\top$ --- mathematically equivalent but uses observations as state components, which the strict DLM definition (DLMwR p.\ 113) forbids. The book's auxiliary form satisfies the DLM constraint while still encoding the AR($p$) dynamics.

trash.title: Lindley Paradox
trash.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Lindley's paradox --- when the two frameworks loudly disagree.}}

A famous case where frequentist and Bayesian conclusions \emph{conflict} on the same data, especially when $n$ is large.

\textbf{Setup.} Test $H_0: \theta = \theta_0$ vs $H_1: \theta \ne \theta_0$, with sample mean $\hat\theta$ near (but not exactly equal to) $\theta_0$.

\textbf{Frequentist machinery.} The test statistic
\[ z = \frac{\hat\theta - \theta_0}{\sigma / \sqrt{n}} \]
contains $\sqrt{n}$. So for any fixed deviation $\hat\theta - \theta_0 \ne 0$, $z$ grows without bound as $n \to \infty$, and the p-value $\to 0$. With enough data, the test \emph{rejects} $H_0$ for any deviation, no matter how small.

\textbf{Bayesian machinery.} Under $H_1$, place a prior $\theta \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \tau^2)$. The Bayes factor is
\[ \text{BF}_{01} \;=\; \frac{p(y \mid H_0)}{p(y \mid H_1)}, \qquad p(y \mid H_1) \;=\; \int p(y \mid \theta)\, \pi(\theta \mid H_1)\, d\theta. \]
The integral averages over \emph{all} $\theta$ in the prior --- including the many values that do not fit $\hat\theta$. With a wide prior, only a tiny sliver near the data has high likelihood; the rest contributes almost nothing. So $H_1$ is \emph{penalised for being a vague hypothesis}: the marginal likelihood is dilute. In large samples this Occam penalty wins unless $H_1$ actually concentrates mass near the observed value.

\textbf{Concrete numbers.} $\sigma = 1$, $\theta_0 = 0$, $\hat\theta = 0.002$, $n = 1{,}000{,}000$, $\tau = 1$:
\[ z \;=\; 2 \;\Rightarrow\; p \;\approx\; 0.045  (\text{frequentist rejects at 5\%}), \]
\[ \text{BF}_{01} \;\approx\; \tau \sqrt{n} \cdot e^{-z^2/2} \;=\; 1000 \cdot e^{-2} \;\approx\; 135  (\text{Bayes factor: data 135}\times \text{ more likely under } H_0). \]

\emph{Same data, opposite conclusions:} frequentist rejects $H_0$, Bayesian strongly supports $H_0$.

\textbf{Why the disagreement?} The two methods answer \emph{different questions}.

$\bullet$ \emph{Frequentist}: "How extreme is the data assuming $H_0$?" With huge $n$, even practically negligible deviations look extreme.

$\bullet$ \emph{Bayesian}: "Which hypothesis predicts the data better, on average?" The vague $H_1$ pays an Occam penalty for spreading prior mass over values that no longer fit.

\textbf{Intuition in one line.}
\[ \text{Frequentist asks: \emph{is the true } \theta \text{ exactly } \theta_0?} \Longleftrightarrow \text{Bayesian asks: \emph{is the data well explained by } \theta_0 \text{ vs by an averaged-over } H_1?} \]

\textbf{Practical message.}

$\bullet$ For \emph{small to moderate $n$} the two frameworks usually agree numerically.

$\bullet$ For \emph{very large $n$} (high-frequency finance, genomics, particle physics), p-values reject everything --- Bayes factors are preferred for model selection.

$\bullet$ This is not a numerical fluke: it is a real difference in what "evidence" means in each framework. Use the framework whose question matches what you actually want to know.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{EXAMPLE SSMs --- HUB: template, worked 2x2 example, map.}}


\begin{keydef}
\textbf{General DLM (linear Gaussian SSM).}

\emph{State equation:} $\;\theta_t \;=\; G_t\, \theta_{t-1} \;+\; w_t,\qquad w_t \stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0,\, W_t),\quad \theta_t \in \mathbb{R}^p.$

\emph{Observation equation:} $\;Y_t \;=\; F_t\, \theta_t \;+\; v_t,\qquad v_t \stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0,\, V_t),\quad Y_t \in \mathbb{R}^q.$

\emph{Independence:} $\{w_t\} \perp \{v_s\}$ and both $\perp\ \theta_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(m_0, C_0)$.
\end{keydef}
.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Summary table --- one model per row, full DLM template per cell (rigorous, repetitive framework).}}

\emph{Every row spells out the same five-step template:} \emph{(1)} state vector $+$ initial $\theta_0$ with component interpretations; \emph{(2)} every component eq (also when constant) with its individual Gaussian noise, joint $w_t \sim \mathcal{N}_d(0, W_t)$, $W_t$ explicit, $\{w_t\} \perp \{v_s\} \perp \theta_0$; \emph{(3)} matrix state eq $\theta_t = G\theta_{t-1} + w_t$ generic $\to$ expanded $G$-matrix $\times \theta_{t-1}$-vector $+ w_t$-vector $\to$ result $\to$ $= \theta_t$; $G$ matrix, $W_t$ matrix, conditional law $\theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1}$; \emph{(4)} obs eq $Y_t = F\theta_t + v_t$ generic $\to$ expanded $F$-vector $\times \theta_t$-vector $\to$ result; $F$, $v_t \sim \mathcal{N}_m(0, V_t)$, $V_t$ explicit, conditional law $Y_t \mid \theta_t$; \emph{(5)} $\mathbb{E}[Y_t]$, $\mathrm{Var}(Y_t)$, forecast bands, stationarity, nesting, when-to-use, R.

\begin{tabular}{l|l|l|l|l|l}
\textbf{Model} & \textbf{(1) State $\theta_t$, init.\ $\theta_0$} & \textbf{(2) Component eqs (incl.\ constants), $w_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, W_t)$, $W_t$, indep.} & \textbf{(3) Matrix state eq (generic $\to$ expand $\to$ result), $G$, $W_t$, $\theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1}$} & \textbf{(4) Obs eq (generic $\to$ expand $\to$ result), $F$, $v_t$, $V_t$, $Y_t \mid \theta_t$} & \textbf{(5) Moments, forecasts, stationarity, nesting, R} \\
\hline
\emph{Global trend (Ex 2a).} \;\emph{(1) Simplest possible trend.} Straight line plus noise. Slope and intercept are fixed numbers. & $\theta = (\underbrace{\mu_0}_{\text{intercept}}, \underbrace{\delta}_{\text{slope}})^\top \in \mathbb{R}^2$, FIXED (deterministic); no $\theta_0$ distribution & $\mu_0 = \mu_0$ (constant in $t$); $\delta = \delta$ (constant in $t$); no internal state noise $\Rightarrow w_t \equiv 0$; $W_t = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr) = 0_{2 \times 2}$; obs noise $v_t$ indep of $\theta$ & $\theta_t = G\theta_{t-1} + w_t = I_2 \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\mu_0 \\ \delta\end{smallmatrix}\bigr) + \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr) = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\mu_0 \\ \delta\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$; $G = I_2 = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$, $W_t = 0_{2 \times 2}$; $\theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1} = \delta(\theta_{t-1})$ (Dirac point mass; state frozen) & $Y_t = F_t\theta_t + v_t = (1, t)\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\mu_0 \\ \delta\end{smallmatrix}\bigr) + v_t = \mu_0 + \delta t + v_t$; $F_t = (1, t)$; $v_t \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, V_t)$, $V_t = \sigma^2$; $Y_t \mid \theta_t \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_0 + \delta t,\, \sigma^2)$ & $\mathbb{E}[Y_t] = \mu_0 + \delta t$; $\mathrm{Var}(Y_t) = \sigma^2$ (constant); forecast bands \emph{flat}; \textbf{non-stat} mean, const var. \emph{Nesting:} $=$ DLR with $W = 0, x_t = t$. \emph{When to use:} residuals iid, trend a clean line. \emph{R:} \texttt{lm(y \textasciitilde\ t)}. \\
\hline
\emph{RW + drift (Ex 2b).} \;\emph{(2) But what if the level itself wanders?} Same average direction, but the realised level is a random walk around the line. & $\theta_t \in \mathbb{R}$ (\textbf{level}); $\theta_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(m_0, C_0)$ & $\theta_t = \theta_{t-1} + \mu + w_t$ (level eq); $w_t \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_w^2)$; $W_t = \sigma_w^2$ (scalar); $\{w_t\}, \{v_s\}, \theta_0$ \emph{mutually independent} (jointly Gaussian $\Rightarrow$ uncorr. $\Leftrightarrow$ indep.) & $\theta_t = G\theta_{t-1} + \mu + w_t = 1 \cdot \theta_{t-1} + \mu + w_t = \theta_{t-1} + \mu + w_t$; $G = 1$, $W_t = \sigma_w^2$; $\theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1} \sim \mathcal{N}(\theta_{t-1} + \mu,\, \sigma_w^2)$ & $Y_t = F\theta_t + v_t = 1 \cdot \theta_t + v_t = \theta_t + v_t$; $F = 1$; $v_t \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, V_t)$, $V_t = \sigma^2$; $v_t \perp w_s, \theta_0$; $Y_t \mid \theta_t \sim \mathcal{N}(\theta_t,\, \sigma^2)$ & $\mathbb{E}[Y_t] = \theta_0 + t\mu$ (same average line); $\mathrm{Var}(Y_t) = t\sigma_w^2 + \sigma^2$ (linear in $t$); forecast bands fan $\propto \sqrt{t}$; \textbf{non-stat} mean and variance. \emph{Nesting:} $=$ LLT with $\sigma_{w_2}^2 = 0$ (slope frozen at $\mu$). \emph{When to use:} long swings off the trend line. \emph{R:} \texttt{dlmModPoly(1)} with drift input. \\
\hline
\emph{LLT / Local linear growth (Ex 5).} \;\emph{(3) What if the slope also wanders?} The ``global'' trend becomes ``local.'' & $\theta_t = (\underbrace{\mu_t}_{\text{level}}, \underbrace{\beta_t}_{\text{slope}})^\top \in \mathbb{R}^2$; $\theta_0 \sim \mathcal{N}_2(m_0, C_0)$ & $\mu_t = \mu_{t-1} + \beta_{t-1} + w_{1,t}$, $w_{1,t} \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_{w_1}^2)$; $\beta_t = \beta_{t-1} + w_{2,t}$, $w_{2,t} \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_{w_2}^2)$; \emph{$w_{1,t} \perp w_{2,t}$ (so $W_t$ diag)}; joint $w_t = (w_{1,t}, w_{2,t})^\top \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}_2(0, W_t)$, $W_t = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\sigma_{w_1}^2 & 0 \\ 0 & \sigma_{w_2}^2\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$; $\{w_t\} \perp \{v_s\} \perp \theta_0$ & $\theta_t = G\theta_{t-1} + w_t = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\mu_{t-1} \\ \beta_{t-1}\end{smallmatrix}\bigr) + \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}w_{1,t} \\ w_{2,t}\end{smallmatrix}\bigr) = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\mu_{t-1} + \beta_{t-1} + w_{1,t} \\ \beta_{t-1} + w_{2,t}\end{smallmatrix}\bigr) = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\mu_t \\ \beta_t\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$; $G = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$, $W_t = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\sigma_{w_1}^2 & 0 \\ 0 & \sigma_{w_2}^2\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$; $\theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1} \sim \mathcal{N}_2(G\theta_{t-1},\, W_t)$ & $Y_t = F\theta_t + v_t = (1, 0)\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\mu_t \\ \beta_t\end{smallmatrix}\bigr) + v_t = \mu_t + v_t$; $F = (1, 0)$; $v_t \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, V_t)$, $V_t = \sigma_v^2$; $v_t \perp w_s, \theta_0$; $Y_t \mid \theta_t \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_t,\, \sigma_v^2)$ & $\mathbb{E}[Y_t] = \mu_0 + t\beta_0$ (in expectation); $\mathrm{Var}(Y_t) \sim t^3$ asymptotic (slope integrates twice); forecast bands fan $\propto t^{3/2}$; \textbf{non-stat}. \emph{Nesting:} $=$ DLR with $x_t = t$, generalises RW + drift. \emph{When to use:} growth rate itself shifts over time. \emph{R:} \texttt{dlmModPoly(2)}. \\
\hline
\emph{DLR (Ex 7).} \;\emph{(4) What if the trend depends on an external variable, not just time?} Replace ``time'' as predictor with any covariate $x_t$; let coefficients drift. & $\theta_t = (\underbrace{\alpha_t}_{\text{intercept}}, \underbrace{\beta_t}_{\text{slope on }x_t})^\top \in \mathbb{R}^2$; $\theta_0 \sim \mathcal{N}_2(m_0, C_0)$ & $\alpha_t = \alpha_{t-1} + w_{1,t}$, $w_{1,t} \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_{w_1}^2)$; $\beta_t = \beta_{t-1} + w_{2,t}$, $w_{2,t} \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_{w_2}^2)$; \emph{$w_{1,t} \perp w_{2,t}$}; joint $w_t \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}_2(0, W_t)$, $W_t = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\sigma_{w_1}^2 & 0 \\ 0 & \sigma_{w_2}^2\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$; mutually $\perp$ with $\{v_s\}, \theta_0$ & $\theta_t = G\theta_{t-1} + w_t = I_2 \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\alpha_{t-1} \\ \beta_{t-1}\end{smallmatrix}\bigr) + \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}w_{1,t} \\ w_{2,t}\end{smallmatrix}\bigr) = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\alpha_{t-1} + w_{1,t} \\ \beta_{t-1} + w_{2,t}\end{smallmatrix}\bigr) = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\alpha_t \\ \beta_t\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$; $G = I_2 = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$, $W_t = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\sigma_{w_1}^2 & 0 \\ 0 & \sigma_{w_2}^2\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$; $\theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1} \sim \mathcal{N}_2(\theta_{t-1},\, W_t)$ & $Y_t = F_t\theta_t + v_t = (1, x_t)\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\alpha_t \\ \beta_t\end{smallmatrix}\bigr) + v_t = \alpha_t + \beta_t x_t + v_t$; $F_t = (1, x_t)$; $v_t \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, V_t)$, $V_t = \sigma_v^2$; $Y_t \mid \theta_t \sim \mathcal{N}(\alpha_t + \beta_t x_t,\, \sigma_v^2)$ & $\mathbb{E}[Y_t]$ path-dep on $x_{1:t}$ (in expectation $\alpha_0 + \beta_0 x_t$); $\mathrm{Var}(Y_t)$ depends on the $x$-path; forecast bands depend on future $x_t$; \textbf{non-stat}. \emph{Most general} in the trend family. \emph{When to use:} time-varying betas, marketing mix, clinical covariates. \emph{R:} \texttt{dlmModReg(X)}. \emph{CAPM:} $Y_t$ excess return of asset, $x_t$ excess return of market. \\
\hline
\emph{Local-level / RW + noise (Ex 1)} & $\theta_t \in \mathbb{R}$ (\textbf{hidden level}); $\theta_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(m_0, C_0)$ & $\theta_t = \theta_{t-1} + w_t$ (level eq); $w_t \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_w^2)$; $W_t = \sigma_w^2$ (scalar); \emph{$w_t \perp v_s$ for all $t, s$, and $\perp \theta_0$ (mutually independent)} & $\theta_t = G\theta_{t-1} + w_t = 1 \cdot \theta_{t-1} + w_t = \theta_{t-1} + w_t$; $G = 1$, $W_t = \sigma_w^2$; $\theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1} \sim \mathcal{N}(\theta_{t-1},\, \sigma_w^2)$ & $Y_t = F\theta_t + v_t = 1 \cdot \theta_t + v_t = \theta_t + v_t$; $F = 1$; $v_t \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, V_t)$, $V_t = \sigma_v^2$; $v_t \perp w_s, \theta_0$; $Y_t \mid \theta_t \sim \mathcal{N}(\theta_t,\, \sigma_v^2)$ & $\mathbb{E}[Y_t] = m_0$ (constant); $\mathrm{Var}(Y_t) = C_0 + t\sigma_w^2 + \sigma_v^2$; forecast bands fan $\propto \sqrt{t}$; \textbf{non-stat} (var grows linearly in $t$). $\sigma_w^2 = 0 \Rightarrow$ iid $\mathcal{N}(\theta_0, \sigma_v^2)$. \emph{R:} \texttt{dlmModPoly(1)} no drift. \\
\hline
\emph{Fixed regression (cross-sec.)} & $\theta = (\underbrace{\alpha}_{\text{intercept}}, \underbrace{\beta}_{\text{slope}})^\top \in \mathbb{R}^2$, FIXED (deterministic); no $\theta_0$ distribution & $\alpha = \alpha$ (constant); $\beta = \beta$ (constant); no internal state noise $\Rightarrow w \equiv 0$; $W = 0_{2 \times 2}$; $v_i \perp v_j$ for $i \ne j$ & $\theta = G\theta + w = I_2 \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\alpha \\ \beta\end{smallmatrix}\bigr) + \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr) = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\alpha \\ \beta\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ (frozen); $G = I_2$, $W = 0_{2 \times 2}$; $\theta \mid \theta = \delta(\theta)$ (Dirac) & $Y_i = F_i\theta + v_i = (1, x_i)\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\alpha \\ \beta\end{smallmatrix}\bigr) + v_i = \alpha + \beta x_i + v_i$; $F_i = (1, x_i)$; $v_i \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, V)$, $V = \sigma^2$; $Y_i \mid \theta \sim \mathcal{N}(\alpha + \beta x_i,\, \sigma^2)$ & $\mathbb{E}[Y_i] = \alpha + \beta x_i$; $\mathrm{Var}(Y_i) = \sigma^2$. \textbf{Degenerate DLM, no time:} coefficients $(\alpha, \beta)$ vary across individuals $i$ (through $x_i$) but \emph{not across time}. \emph{R:} \texttt{lm(y \textasciitilde\ x)}. \\
\hline
\emph{AR(1) deg.\ DLM (Ex 3)} & $\theta_t \in \mathbb{R}$ (\textbf{observation itself}, $= Y_t$); $\theta_0$ given (or stat.\ start $\theta_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\, \sigma^2/(1-\varphi^2))$) & $\theta_t = \varphi\theta_{t-1} + w_t$; $w_t \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$; $W_t = \sigma^2$ (scalar); $\{w_t\}$ iid, $w_t \perp \theta_0$; degenerate obs noise: $v_t \equiv 0$ & $\theta_t = G\theta_{t-1} + w_t = \varphi \cdot \theta_{t-1} + w_t$; $G = \varphi$ (scalar), $W_t = \sigma^2$; $\theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1} \sim \mathcal{N}(\varphi\theta_{t-1},\, \sigma^2)$ & $Y_t = F\theta_t + v_t = 1 \cdot \theta_t + 0 = \theta_t$; $F = 1$; $v_t \equiv 0$, $V_t = 0$ (deg.); $Y_t \mid \theta_t = \theta_t$ (point mass, no obs noise) & Stat iff $|\varphi| < 1$. \emph{In stat case:} $\mathbb{E}[Y_t] = 0$, $\mathrm{Var}(Y_t) = \sigma^2/(1 - \varphi^2)$, $\rho(h) = \varphi^{|h|}$; geometric ACF decay. \emph{R:} \texttt{arima(y, c(1, 0, 0))}. \\
\hline
\emph{AR(2) deg.\ DLM} & $\theta_t = (\underbrace{\theta_{1,t}}_{= Y_t}, \underbrace{\theta_{2,t}}_{\text{aux (carries past)}})^\top \in \mathbb{R}^2$; $\theta_0$ given & $\theta_{1,t} = \phi_1\theta_{1,t-1} + \theta_{2,t-1} + w_t$, $w_t \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$; $\theta_{2,t} = \phi_2\theta_{1,t-1}$ (deterministic, no shock); joint state shock $(w_t, 0)^\top \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}_2(0, W_t)$, $W_t = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\sigma^2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ (singular); $w_t \perp \theta_0$ & $\theta_t = G\theta_{t-1} + (w_t, 0)^\top = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\phi_1 & 1 \\ \phi_2 & 0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\theta_{1,t-1} \\ \theta_{2,t-1}\end{smallmatrix}\bigr) + \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}w_t \\ 0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr) = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\phi_1\theta_{1,t-1} + \theta_{2,t-1} + w_t \\ \phi_2\theta_{1,t-1}\end{smallmatrix}\bigr) = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\theta_{1,t} \\ \theta_{2,t}\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$; $G = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\phi_1 & 1 \\ \phi_2 & 0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$, $W_t = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\sigma^2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$; $\theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1} \sim \mathcal{N}_2(G\theta_{t-1},\, W_t)$ (singular: $0$-variance in row 2) & $Y_t = F\theta_t + v_t = (1, 0)\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\theta_{1,t} \\ \theta_{2,t}\end{smallmatrix}\bigr) + 0 = \theta_{1,t}$; $F = (1, 0)$; $v_t \equiv 0$, $V_t = 0$ (deg.); $Y_t \mid \theta_t = \theta_{1,t}$ (point mass) & Stat iff $(\phi_1, \phi_2)$ in stability triangle: $\phi_1 + \phi_2 < 1$, $\phi_2 - \phi_1 < 1$, $|\phi_2| < 1$. \emph{In stat case:} $\mathbb{E}[Y_t] = 0$, $\mathrm{Var}(Y_t) = \dfrac{(1 - \phi_2)\sigma^2}{(1 + \phi_2)\bigl((1 - \phi_2)^2 - \phi_1^2\bigr)}$. \emph{R:} \texttt{arima(y, c(2, 0, 0))}. \\
\hline
\emph{VAR(1)} & $\theta_t = (\underbrace{X_t}_{\text{series 1}}, \underbrace{Y_t}_{\text{series 2}})^\top \in \mathbb{R}^2$ ($=$ obs directly, deg.); $\theta_0$ given & $X_t = \phi_{11}X_{t-1} + \phi_{12}Y_{t-1} + w_{1,t}$; $Y_t = \phi_{21}X_{t-1} + \phi_{22}Y_{t-1} + w_{2,t}$; each $w_{i,t}$ Gaussian; joint $w_t = (w_{1,t}, w_{2,t})^\top \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}_2(0, \Sigma)$, $W_t = \Sigma = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\sigma_1^2 & \sigma_{12} \\ \sigma_{12} & \sigma_2^2\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ (\emph{generally non-diag $\Rightarrow$ correlated shocks}); $w_t \perp \theta_0$ & $\theta_t = G\theta_{t-1} + w_t = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\phi_{11} & \phi_{12} \\ \phi_{21} & \phi_{22}\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}X_{t-1} \\ Y_{t-1}\end{smallmatrix}\bigr) + \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}w_{1,t} \\ w_{2,t}\end{smallmatrix}\bigr) = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\phi_{11}X_{t-1} + \phi_{12}Y_{t-1} + w_{1,t} \\ \phi_{21}X_{t-1} + \phi_{22}Y_{t-1} + w_{2,t}\end{smallmatrix}\bigr) = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}X_t \\ Y_t\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$; $G = \Phi = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\phi_{11} & \phi_{12} \\ \phi_{21} & \phi_{22}\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$, $W_t = \Sigma$; $\theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1} \sim \mathcal{N}_2(\Phi\theta_{t-1},\, \Sigma)$ & $\mathbf{Y}_t = F\theta_t + v_t = I_2 \theta_t + 0 = \theta_t$; $F = I_2 = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$; $v_t \equiv 0$, $V_t = 0_{2 \times 2}$ (deg.); $\mathbf{Y}_t \mid \theta_t = \theta_t$ (point mass) & Stat iff eigenvalues of $\Phi$ inside unit circle. \emph{In stat case:} $\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{Y}_t] = 0$, $\mathrm{Var}(\mathbf{Y}_t) = \mathrm{vec}^{-1}\!\bigl((I - \Phi \otimes \Phi)^{-1} \mathrm{vec}(\Sigma)\bigr)$; Cross-coupling in $G$ enables Granger causality. \emph{R:} \texttt{vars::VAR(y, p=1)}. \\
\hline
\emph{SUTSE (LLT stacked)} & $\theta_t = (\underbrace{\mu_t^X, \mu_t^Y}_{\text{levels (series X, Y)}}, \underbrace{\beta_t^X, \beta_t^Y}_{\text{slopes (series X, Y)}})^\top \in \mathbb{R}^4$; $\theta_0 \sim \mathcal{N}_4(m_0, C_0)$ & $\mu_t^X = \mu_{t-1}^X + \beta_{t-1}^X + w_{1,t}$; $\mu_t^Y = \mu_{t-1}^Y + \beta_{t-1}^Y + w_{2,t}$; $\beta_t^X = \beta_{t-1}^X + w_{3,t}$; $\beta_t^Y = \beta_{t-1}^Y + w_{4,t}$; each $w_{i,t}$ Gaussian; joint $w_t = (w_{1,t},w_{2,t},w_{3,t},w_{4,t})^\top \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}_4(0, W_t)$, $W_t = \mathrm{blkdiag}(W_\mu, W_\beta) = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}W_\mu & 0 \\ 0 & W_\beta\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ with $W_\mu, W_\beta$ each $2 \times 2$ possibly non-diag (\emph{cross-series shock corr.\ via off-diag of each block}); $\{w_t\} \perp \{v_s\} \perp \theta_0$ & $\theta_t = G\theta_{t-1} + w_t = (G_{\mathrm{LLT}} \otimes I_2)\theta_{t-1} + w_t = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\mu_{t-1}^X + \beta_{t-1}^X + w_{1,t} \\ \mu_{t-1}^Y + \beta_{t-1}^Y + w_{2,t} \\ \beta_{t-1}^X + w_{3,t} \\ \beta_{t-1}^Y + w_{4,t}\end{smallmatrix}\bigr) = (\mu_t^X, \mu_t^Y, \beta_t^X, \beta_t^Y)^\top$; $G = G_{\mathrm{LLT}} \otimes I_2$, $W_t = \mathrm{blkdiag}(W_\mu, W_\beta)$; $\theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1} \sim \mathcal{N}_4(G\theta_{t-1},\, W_t)$ & $\mathbf{Y}_t = F\theta_t + v_t = [I_2 \mid 0]\, \theta_t + v_t = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\mu_t^X \\ \mu_t^Y\end{smallmatrix}\bigr) + v_t$; $F = [I_2 \mid 0]$ (picks the two levels); $v_t \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}_2(0, V_t)$, $V_t$ possibly non-diag (e.g.\ $\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\sigma_{v_1}^2 & \sigma_{v_{12}} \\ \sigma_{v_{12}} & \sigma_{v_2}^2\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$); $\mathbf{Y}_t \mid \theta_t \sim \mathcal{N}_2(F\theta_t,\, V_t)$ & $\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{Y}_t] = (m_{\mu,0}^X + t m_{\beta,0}^X,\, m_{\mu,0}^Y + t m_{\beta,0}^Y)^\top$; $\mathrm{Var}$ grows $\sim t^3$ per series; \textbf{non-stat}. Cross-series link in $W$ (state noise) not in $G$. Petris \S3.3.2. \emph{R:} \texttt{dlm} with custom $F, G, W, V$. \\
\hline
\emph{SUR (dynamic, common $x_t$)} & $\theta_t = (\underbrace{\alpha_t^X, \alpha_t^Y}_{\text{intercepts (X, Y)}}, \underbrace{\beta_t^X, \beta_t^Y}_{\text{slopes on }x_t})^\top \in \mathbb{R}^4$; $\theta_0 \sim \mathcal{N}_4(m_0, C_0)$ & $\alpha_t^X = \alpha_{t-1}^X + w_{1,t}$; $\alpha_t^Y = \alpha_{t-1}^Y + w_{2,t}$; $\beta_t^X = \beta_{t-1}^X + w_{3,t}$; $\beta_t^Y = \beta_{t-1}^Y + w_{4,t}$ (each coeff is RW with own Gaussian shock); joint $w_t = (w_{1,t},w_{2,t},w_{3,t},w_{4,t})^\top \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}_4(0, W_t)$, $W_t = \mathrm{blkdiag}(W_\alpha, W_\beta) = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}W_\alpha & 0 \\ 0 & W_\beta\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ with off-diag in each $2 \times 2$ block (\emph{cross-eqn coefficient-shock corr.}); $\{w_t\} \perp \{v_s\} \perp \theta_0$ & $\theta_t = G\theta_{t-1} + w_t = I_4 \theta_{t-1} + w_t = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\alpha_{t-1}^X + w_{1,t} \\ \alpha_{t-1}^Y + w_{2,t} \\ \beta_{t-1}^X + w_{3,t} \\ \beta_{t-1}^Y + w_{4,t}\end{smallmatrix}\bigr) = (\alpha_t^X, \alpha_t^Y, \beta_t^X, \beta_t^Y)^\top$; $G = I_4$, $W_t = \mathrm{blkdiag}(W_\alpha, W_\beta)$; $\theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1} \sim \mathcal{N}_4(\theta_{t-1},\, W_t)$ & $\mathbf{Y}_t = F_t\theta_t + v_t = \bigl((1, x_t) \otimes I_2\bigr)\theta_t + v_t = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\alpha_t^X + \beta_t^X x_t \\ \alpha_t^Y + \beta_t^Y x_t\end{smallmatrix}\bigr) + v_t$; $F_t = (1, x_t) \otimes I_2 = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}1 & 0 & x_t & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & x_t\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$; $v_t \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}_2(0, V_t)$, \emph{$V_t$ possibly non-diag} (Zellner cross-eqn residual corr.); $\mathbf{Y}_t \mid \theta_t \sim \mathcal{N}_2(F_t\theta_t,\, V_t)$ & $\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{Y}_t]^j = m_{\alpha,0}^j + m_{\beta,0}^j x_t$ ($j \in \{X, Y\}$); $\mathrm{Var}$ path-dep on $x_{1:t}$, grows; \textbf{non-stat}. Link in BOTH $W$ (state) and $V$ (obs). CAPM with shared market regressor $x_t$. Petris \S3.3.3. \emph{R:} \texttt{dlm} custom with Kronecker. \\
\hline
\emph{Superposition (additive components)} & stacked: $\theta_t = (\underbrace{\theta_{1,t}^\top}_{\text{comp.\ 1 state}}, \dots, \underbrace{\theta_{k,t}^\top}_{\text{comp.\ }k\text{ state}})^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{p_1 + \cdots + p_k}$; $\theta_0$ stacked from comp.\ priors & per component $j = 1, \dots, k$: $\theta_{j,t} = G_j\theta_{j,t-1} + w_{j,t}$, $w_{j,t} \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}_{p_j}(0, W_{j,t})$; \emph{$w_{j,t} \perp w_{l,t}$ for $j \ne l$} (block-diag $W$); joint $w_t = (w_{1,t}^\top, \dots, w_{k,t}^\top)^\top \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, W_t)$, $W_t = \mathrm{blkdiag}(W_{1,t}, \dots, W_{k,t})$; $\{w_t\} \perp \{v_s\} \perp \theta_0$ & $\theta_t = G\theta_{t-1} + w_t = \mathrm{blkdiag}(G_1, \dots, G_k)\theta_{t-1} + w_t = (G_1\theta_{1,t-1} + w_{1,t},\, \dots,\, G_k\theta_{k,t-1} + w_{k,t})^\top = (\theta_{1,t}^\top, \dots, \theta_{k,t}^\top)^\top$; $G = \mathrm{blkdiag}(G_1, \dots, G_k)$, $W_t = \mathrm{blkdiag}(W_{1,t}, \dots, W_{k,t})$; $\theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1} \sim \mathcal{N}(G\theta_{t-1},\, W_t)$ & $Y_t = F\theta_t + v_t = [F_1 \mid \dots \mid F_k]\, \theta_t + v_t = \sum_j F_j \theta_{j,t} + v_t$; $F = [F_1 \mid \dots \mid F_k]$ (row-concat); $v_t = \sum_j v_{j,t} \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, V_t)$, $V_t = \sum_j V_{j,t}$ (sum of indep component obs noises); $Y_t \mid \theta_t \sim \mathcal{N}(F\theta_t,\, V_t)$ & $\mathbb{E}[Y_t] = \sum_j F_j \mathbb{E}[\theta_{j,t}]$; $\mathrm{Var}(Y_t) = V_t + \sum_j F_j \mathrm{Var}(\theta_{j,t}) F_j^\top$; stat iff every component is stat. Classic BSM $=$ LLT $+$ seasonal $+$ irregular. \emph{R:} \texttt{dlmModPoly() + dlmModSeas() + dlmModReg()}. \\
\hline
\emph{Trend + AR(2) cycle (worked above, last row)} & $\theta_t = (\underbrace{T_t}_{\text{trend (RW)}}, \underbrace{C_t}_{\text{cycle (AR(2))}}, \underbrace{C_{t-1}}_{\text{aux lag}})^\top \in \mathbb{R}^3$; $\theta_0 \sim \mathcal{N}_3(m_0, C_0)$ & $T_t = T_{t-1} + u_t$, $u_t \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_T^2)$; $C_t = \phi_1 C_{t-1} + \phi_2 C_{t-2} + r_t$, $r_t \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_C^2)$; aux $C_{t-1}$ deterministic copy (no shock); \emph{$u_t \perp r_t$ (so $W_t$ block-diag)}; joint $w_t = (u_t, r_t, 0)^\top \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}_3(0, W_t)$, $W_t = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\sigma_T^2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \sigma_C^2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$; $\{u_t, r_t\} \perp \{v_s\} \perp \theta_0$ & $\theta_t = G\theta_{t-1} + w_t = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \phi_1 & \phi_2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}T_{t-1} \\ C_{t-1} \\ C_{t-2}\end{smallmatrix}\bigr) + \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}u_t \\ r_t \\ 0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr) = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}T_{t-1} + u_t \\ \phi_1 C_{t-1} + \phi_2 C_{t-2} + r_t \\ C_{t-1}\end{smallmatrix}\bigr) = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}T_t \\ C_t \\ C_{t-1}\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$; $G = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \phi_1 & \phi_2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$, $W_t = \mathrm{diag}(\sigma_T^2, \sigma_C^2, 0)$; $\theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1} \sim \mathcal{N}_3(G\theta_{t-1},\, W_t)$ & $Y_t = F\theta_t + v_t = (1, 1, 0)\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}T_t \\ C_t \\ C_{t-1}\end{smallmatrix}\bigr) + v_t = T_t + C_t + v_t$; $F = (1, 1, 0)$; $v_t \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, V_t)$, $V_t = \sigma_\nu^2$ (scalar); $Y_t \mid \theta_t \sim \mathcal{N}(T_t + C_t,\, \sigma_\nu^2)$ & $\mathbb{E}[Y_t] = m_{T,0} + 0$ (assuming AR(2) cycle stationary, mean-zero); $\mathrm{Var}(Y_t) = C_{T,0} + t\sigma_T^2 + \mathrm{Var}(C_t) + \sigma_\nu^2$; \textbf{non-stat} (trend integrates). Superposition of RW trend $+$ AR(2) cycle; aux slot for AR(2) Markovianisation. \emph{R:} \texttt{dlmModPoly(1) + dlmModARMA(ar=c(phi1, phi2))}. \\
\end{tabular}

\emph{Conventions.} $e_1 = (1, 0, \dots, 0)^\top$. Lower-case $w_t, w_{i,t}, v_t, u_t, r_t, \nu_t$ are Gaussian noises. \emph{Degenerate DLM} ($V_t = 0$, $v_t \equiv 0$): obs eq collapses to $Y_t = F\theta_t$ (state observed exactly --- AR family, VAR). ``Mutually independent'' for jointly Gaussian variables $\Leftrightarrow$ pairwise uncorrelated. $\delta(\cdot)$ is a point mass (Dirac).

trash.title: Example 2: Trend DLMs: global, RW+drift, LLT / Local linear growth, DLR (one note)
VAR (Vector AutoRegression) as state-space model
trash.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{VECTOR AUTOREGRESSION (VAR) AS STATE-SPACE MODEL.}}

Multivariate extension of AR: each component depends on lagged values of \emph{every} component (its own and the others'). Captures \emph{joint dynamics} (Granger causality, impulse-response analysis).

\emph{Footnote --- book status.} Petris (\S3.3.7, p.\ 141) explicitly notes ``\emph{we will not treat VAR models or cointegration in this book}'' --- VAR is mentioned only as a special case of multivariate ARMA (eq.\ 3.50, no MA part). The DLM below is the natural specialization of that ARMA-DLM with $q = 0, p = 1$: state $=$ current vector, $G = \Phi$, $F = I$, $V = 0$. Standard treatment in econometrics texts (L\"utkepohl 2005, Canova 2007).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{VAR(1) on two series $X, Y$ --- 4-step DLM template.}}

\emph{(1) State (with components).} $\theta_t = (X_t,\, Y_t)^\top \in \mathbb{R}^2$, where $X_t$ and $Y_t$ are the two observed series at time $t$.

\emph{(2) Component equations.}
\[ X_t \;=\; \phi_{11}\, X_{t-1} + \phi_{12}\, Y_{t-1} + w_{1,t}, \]
\[ Y_t \;=\; \phi_{21}\, X_{t-1} + \phi_{22}\, Y_{t-1} + w_{2,t}, \]
with $(w_{1,t},\, w_{2,t})^\top \sim \mathcal{N}_2(0,\, \Sigma)$, $\Sigma = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\sigma_1^2 & \sigma_{12} \\ \sigma_{12} & \sigma_2^2\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$.

\emph{Reading.} Each line shows: $X_t$ depends on $X_{t-1}$ AND $Y_{t-1}$ (own lag $+$ cross-lag); symmetrically for $Y_t$. Off-diagonal $\phi_{12}, \phi_{21}$ encode the cross-influence; $\sigma_{12}$ encodes contemporaneous correlation in the shocks.

\emph{(3) Matrix state equation.}
\[ \theta_t \;=\; G\, \theta_{t-1} + w_t \;=\; \begin{pmatrix}\phi_{11} & \phi_{12} \\ \phi_{21} & \phi_{22}\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}X_{t-1} \\ Y_{t-1}\end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix}w_{1,t} \\ w_{2,t}\end{pmatrix} \;=\; \begin{pmatrix}\phi_{11} X_{t-1} + \phi_{12} Y_{t-1} + w_{1,t} \\ \phi_{21} X_{t-1} + \phi_{22} Y_{t-1} + w_{2,t}\end{pmatrix} \;=\; \begin{pmatrix}X_t \\ Y_t\end{pmatrix}. \]
$G = \Phi = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\phi_{11} & \phi_{12} \\ \phi_{21} & \phi_{22}\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$, and $w_t \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}_2(0,\, W_t)$ with $W_t = \Sigma$.

\emph{Distributional form.} $\theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1} \sim \mathcal{N}_2\!\bigl(\Phi\, \theta_{t-1},\; \Sigma\bigr)$.

\emph{(4) Observation equation.} The state IS the observation (VAR is directly observed):
\[ \mathbf{Y}_t \;=\; (X_t,\, Y_t)^\top =  F\, \theta_t + v_t \;=\; I_2\, \theta_t + 0 \;=\; \theta_t \]
with $F = I_2$, $V = 0$ (degenerate DLM --- like AR but multivariate).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Why VAR matters.}}

$\bullet$ \emph{Multivariate dependence.} Each component depends not only on its own lags but on every other component's lags. Captures Granger causality, impulse responses, dynamic interactions.

$\bullet$ \emph{Workhorse of macroeconometrics.} Sims (1980) introduced VAR for empirical macro --- modelling joint dynamics of GDP, inflation, interest rates, etc.

$\bullet$ \emph{Filtering / forecasting via Kalman.} Once in DLM form, all the usual machinery applies: filter for state, forecast at horizon $h$, MLE on $(\Phi, \Sigma)$ via the prediction-error decomposition.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Connections.}}

$\bullet$ \emph{$q = 1$:} VAR collapses to AR(1) --- single scalar series.

$\bullet$ \emph{Adding measurement noise} ($V > 0$): "VAR + noise" or dynamic factor model (DFM) structure; common in finance for latent factors driving observed prices.

$\bullet$ \emph{HMM analog:} discrete-state version is multi-state HMM with state-dependent emissions.

trash.title: SUTSE (Seemingly Unrelated Time Series) as state-space model
trash.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{SEEMINGLY UNRELATED TIME SERIES EQUATIONS (SUTSE) --- Petris \S3.3.2, p.\ 127.}}


SUTSE = stack $m$ LLTs (each piece has latent level + slope, driven internally)   

Stack $m$ structural univariate DLMs (each series has its OWN level + slope --- a Local Linear Trend), then let the \emph{state-noise shocks correlate across series}. 

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{SUTSE on two series $X, Y$ (each Local Linear Trend) --- 4-step DLM template.}}

\emph{(1) State (with components).} $\theta_t = (\mu_t^X,\, \mu_t^Y,\, \beta_t^X,\, \beta_t^Y)^\top \in \mathbb{R}^4$, where $\mu_t^{X}, \mu_t^{Y}$ are the (latent) \emph{levels} of the two series and $\beta_t^{X}, \beta_t^{Y}$ are their \emph{slopes}. Book convention: group by component (all levels first, then all slopes).

\emph{Footnote --- equivalent matrix form.} You can organize the same state as a $2 \times 2$ \emph{matrix} $\Theta_t = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\mu_t^X & \beta_t^X \\ \mu_t^Y & \beta_t^Y\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$. The first column is component vector 

\emph{(2) Component equations (each series is its own LLT).}
\[ \mu_t^X = \mu_{t-1}^X + \beta_{t-1}^X + w_{1,t}, \qquad \mu_t^Y = \mu_{t-1}^Y + \beta_{t-1}^Y + w_{2,t}, \]
\[ \beta_t^X = \beta_{t-1}^X + w_{3,t}, \qquad \beta_t^Y = \beta_{t-1}^Y + w_{4,t}, \]
with $(w_{1,t}, w_{2,t}, w_{3,t}, w_{4,t})^\top \sim \mathcal{N}_4(0,\, W)$ and \emph{block-diagonal}
\[ W = \begin{pmatrix} W_\mu & 0 \\ 0 & W_\beta \end{pmatrix}, \quad W_\mu = \begin{pmatrix}\sigma_{\mu_X}^2 & \sigma_{\mu_{XY}} \\ \sigma_{\mu_{XY}} & \sigma_{\mu_Y}^2\end{pmatrix}, \quad W_\beta = \begin{pmatrix}\sigma_{\beta_X}^2 & \sigma_{\beta_{XY}} \\ \sigma_{\beta_{XY}} & \sigma_{\beta_Y}^2\end{pmatrix}. \]

\emph{Reading.} $\mu_t^X$ depends \textbf{only} on its own past $(\mu_{t-1}^X, \beta_{t-1}^X)$, never on $\mu_{t-1}^Y$. Same for the others --- \emph{no cross-coupling in the dynamics}. The cross-series link lives in the off-diagonals $\sigma_{\mu_{XY}}$ and $\sigma_{\beta_{XY}}$: shocks to the two levels (and to the two slopes) are contemporaneously correlated.

\emph{(3) Matrix state equation.}
\[ \theta_t \;=\; G\, \theta_{t-1} + w_t \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \mu_{t-1}^X \\ \mu_{t-1}^Y \\ \beta_{t-1}^X \\ \beta_{t-1}^Y \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} w_{1,t} \\ w_{2,t} \\ w_{3,t} \\ w_{4,t} \end{pmatrix} \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} \mu_{t-1}^X + \beta_{t-1}^X + w_{1,t} \\ \mu_{t-1}^Y + \beta_{t-1}^Y + w_{2,t} \\ \beta_{t-1}^X + w_{3,t} \\ \beta_{t-1}^Y + w_{4,t} \end{pmatrix} \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} \mu_t^X \\ \mu_t^Y \\ \beta_t^X \\ \beta_t^Y \end{pmatrix}. \]
Equivalently $G = G_{\mathrm{LLT}} \otimes I_2$ with $G_{\mathrm{LLT}} = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ (Kronecker form, book eq.\ 3.40). State-noise distribution: $w_t \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}_4(0,\, W_t)$ with $W_t = \mathrm{blkdiag}(W_\mu, W_\beta)$ as in step (2).

\emph{Distributional form.} $\theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1} \sim \mathcal{N}_4\!\bigl(G\, \theta_{t-1},\; W\bigr)$, with $W = \mathrm{blkdiag}(W_\mu, W_\beta)$ as above.

\emph{(4) Observation equation (only the levels are observed).}
\[ Y_t = \begin{pmatrix} X_t \\ Y_t \end{pmatrix} \;=\; \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}}_{F} \theta_t + \begin{pmatrix} v_{1,t} \\ v_{2,t} \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \begin{pmatrix} v_{1,t} \\ v_{2,t} \end{pmatrix} \sim \mathcal{N}_2(0,\, V), \]
Obs-noise distribution: $v_t \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}_2(0,\, V_t)$ with $V_t = V$, a $2 \times 2$ matrix (book allows $V$ non-diagonal, adding a \emph{further} cross-series link in obs noise on top of the main one in $W$).

\emph{Multiplying out $F\, \theta_t$:}
\[ F\, \theta_t \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} \mu_t^X \\ \mu_t^Y \end{pmatrix} \;\Longrightarrow\; \begin{pmatrix} X_t \\ Y_t \end{pmatrix} \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} \mu_t^X + v_{1,t} \\ \mu_t^Y + v_{2,t} \end{pmatrix}. \]

\emph{Distributional form.} $\bigl(X_t, Y_t\bigr)^\top \mid \theta_t \sim \mathcal{N}_2\!\bigl(F\, \theta_t,\; V\bigr)$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Contrast with VAR.}}

\begin{tabular}{l|l|l}
& \textbf{VAR(1)} & \textbf{SUTSE} \\
\hline
\emph{State} & $(X_t, Y_t)$ directly & $(\mu_t^X, \mu_t^Y, \beta_t^X, \beta_t^Y)$ (latent) \\
\emph{Transition $G$} & dense ($\phi_{12}, \phi_{21} \ne 0$) & block, no cross-series coupling \\
\emph{Source of link} & lagged cross-effects in $G$ & shock correlation in $W$ \\
\emph{Granger causality} & possible & no (no lagged-$X$ effect on $Y$) \\
\emph{Observation $F$} & $I_2$ (state $=$ obs) & picks out levels only \\
\end{tabular}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Why SUTSE is useful.}}

$\bullet$ \emph{Efficiency gain over separate equations.} If you fit each series on its own (ignoring the cross-series covariances), estimates are still consistent but lose efficiency. Using the joint covariance gives smaller standard errors --- Zellner's classic SUR result (1962).

$\bullet$ \emph{Common shocks.} The off-diagonals in $W_\mu, W_\beta$ capture \emph{shared exposure to a common factor} (oil price shock affecting both GDP and inflation; market-wide shock to two stocks).

$\bullet$ \emph{Sparser than VAR.} If you believe the series are dynamically independent but driven by common shocks, SUTSE uses fewer parameters --- no off-diagonal entries in $G$, only correlations in the noise.




\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Special cases.}}

$\bullet$ $W_\mu, W_\beta$ both diagonal and $V$ diagonal: SUTSE collapses to \emph{two independent univariate LLTs} --- can be fit separately.

$\bullet$ $W_\mu = 0$: levels follow integrated random walks (slopes drift, levels accumulate). Common simplification.

$\bullet$ $m = 1$: collapses to a single Local Linear Trend (Example 5).

$\bullet$ All slopes $\beta_t^{X} = \beta_t^{Y} = 0$ and $W_\beta = 0$: collapses to two correlated random walks (no trend), with link via $W_\mu$.

trash.title: SUR (dynamic, multivariate) as state-space model
trash.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{SEEMINGLY UNRELATED REGRESSIONS (SUR), DYNAMIC --- Petris \S3.3.3, p.\ 132.}}

now you have m assets = m time series $y_i$

SUR = stack $m$ DLRs (each piece is a regression on an external $x_t$), then let the noise covariances correlate across equations. 

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{SUR on two series $X, Y$ with common regressor $x_t$ --- 4-step DLM template.}}

\emph{(1) State (with components --- book convention: group by component type).} $\theta_t = (\alpha_t^X,\, \alpha_t^Y,\, \beta_t^X,\, \beta_t^Y)^\top \in \mathbb{R}^4$, where $\alpha_t^X, \alpha_t^Y$ are the (drifting) \emph{intercepts} of the two equations and $\beta_t^X, \beta_t^Y$ are the (drifting) \emph{slopes} on the common regressor $x_t$.

\emph{(2) Component equations (each coefficient is a random walk).}
\[ \alpha_t^X = \alpha_{t-1}^X + w_{1,t}, \qquad \alpha_t^Y = \alpha_{t-1}^Y + w_{2,t}, \]
\[ \beta_t^X = \beta_{t-1}^X + w_{3,t}, \qquad \beta_t^Y = \beta_{t-1}^Y + w_{4,t}, \]
note here we keep the slope seprate form the intercept, this is a conceptual point, we could have put them together, but the idea is that alfa and beta are decsribign two very different things
with $(w_{1,t}, w_{2,t}, w_{3,t}, w_{4,t})^\top \sim \mathcal{N}_4(0,\, W)$ and \emph{block-diagonal}
\[ W = \begin{pmatrix} W_\alpha & 0 \\ 0 & W_\beta \end{pmatrix}, \quad W_\alpha = \begin{pmatrix}\sigma_{\alpha_X}^2 & \sigma_{\alpha_{XY}} \\ \sigma_{\alpha_{XY}} & \sigma_{\alpha_Y}^2\end{pmatrix}, \quad W_\beta = \begin{pmatrix}\sigma_{\beta_X}^2 & \sigma_{\beta_{XY}} \\ \sigma_{\beta_{XY}} & \sigma_{\beta_Y}^2\end{pmatrix}. \]
\emph{Primary SUR link in state noise:} off-diagonals $\sigma_{\alpha_{XY}}, \sigma_{\beta_{XY}}$ couple the intercept shocks across series and the slope shocks across series.

\emph{(3) Matrix state equation.}
\[ \theta_t \;=\; G\, \theta_{t-1} + w_t \;=\; I_4 \begin{pmatrix} \alpha_{t-1}^X \\ \alpha_{t-1}^Y \\ \beta_{t-1}^X \\ \beta_{t-1}^Y \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} w_{1,t} \\ w_{2,t} \\ w_{3,t} \\ w_{4,t} \end{pmatrix} \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} \alpha_{t-1}^X + w_{1,t} \\ \alpha_{t-1}^Y + w_{2,t} \\ \beta_{t-1}^X + w_{3,t} \\ \beta_{t-1}^Y + w_{4,t} \end{pmatrix} \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} \alpha_t^X \\ \alpha_t^Y \\ \beta_t^X \\ \beta_t^Y \end{pmatrix}. \]
$G = I_4$ (coefficients evolve independently in mean); state-noise distribution $w_t \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}_4(0,\, W_t)$ with $W_t = \mathrm{blkdiag}(W_\alpha, W_\beta)$ as in step (2). All cross-series coupling is pushed into $W$.

\emph{Distributional form.} $\theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1} \sim \mathcal{N}_4\!\bigl(\theta_{t-1},\; W\bigr)$, with $W = \mathrm{blkdiag}(W_\alpha, W_\beta)$ as above.

\emph{(4) Observation equation (Kronecker form, book eq.\ 3.42).}
\[ Y_t = \begin{pmatrix} X_t \\ Y_t \end{pmatrix} \;=\; \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & x_t & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & x_t \end{pmatrix}}_{F_t \;=\; (1,\,x_t) \,\otimes\, I_2} \theta_t + \begin{pmatrix} v_{1,t} \\ v_{2,t} \end{pmatrix}, \quad \begin{pmatrix} v_{1,t} \\ v_{2,t} \end{pmatrix} \sim \mathcal{N}_2(0,\, V), \]
with $v_t \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}_2(0,\, V_t)$ and $V_t = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\sigma_{v_X}^2 & \sigma_{v_{XY}} \\ \sigma_{v_{XY}} & \sigma_{v_Y}^2\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ also possibly non-diagonal (secondary cross-series link).

\emph{Multiplying out $F_t\, \theta_t$:}
\[ F_t\, \theta_t = \begin{pmatrix} \alpha_t^X + \beta_t^X\, x_t \\ \alpha_t^Y + \beta_t^Y\, x_t \end{pmatrix} \;\Longrightarrow\; \begin{pmatrix} X_t \\ Y_t \end{pmatrix} \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} \alpha_t^X + \beta_t^X\, x_t + v_{1,t} \\ \alpha_t^Y + \beta_t^Y\, x_t + v_{2,t} \end{pmatrix}. \]

\emph{Distributional form.} $\bigl(X_t, Y_t\bigr)^\top \mid \theta_t \sim \mathcal{N}_2\!\bigl(F_t\, \theta_t,\; V\bigr)$.
Both equations use the SAME regressor $x_t$ but with their own (drifting) intercept and slope --- "seemingly unrelated" because they appear independent yet are linked through correlated noises.


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{General $m$-asset SUR --- compact Kronecker form.}}

For $m$ response series $Y_t^{(1)}, \dots, Y_t^{(m)}$ regressed on a common scalar $x_t$:

\emph{(1) State.} $\theta_t = \bigl(\alpha_t^{(1)}, \dots, \alpha_t^{(m)},\, \beta_t^{(1)}, \dots, \beta_t^{(m)}\bigr)^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{2m}$.

\emph{(2) Component equations.} For each $i = 1, \dots, m$:
\[ \alpha_t^{(i)} = \alpha_{t-1}^{(i)} + w_{\alpha,t}^{(i)}, \qquad \beta_t^{(i)} = \beta_{t-1}^{(i)} + w_{\beta,t}^{(i)}, \]
\[ \bigl(w_{\alpha,t}^{(1)}, \dots, w_{\alpha,t}^{(m)},\, w_{\beta,t}^{(1)}, \dots, w_{\beta,t}^{(m)}\bigr)^\top \sim \mathcal{N}_{2m}(0,\, W), \quad W = \mathrm{blkdiag}(W_\alpha, W_\beta), \]
with $W_\alpha, W_\beta$ each $m \times m$ (typically non-diagonal --- the primary cross-asset link).

\emph{(3) Matrix state equation.} $G = I_{2m}$, so
\[ \theta_t = G\, \theta_{t-1} + w_t, \qquad \theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1} \sim \mathcal{N}_{2m}(\theta_{t-1},\, W). \]

\emph{(4) Observation equation.} $F_t = (1, x_t) \otimes I_m$, an $m \times 2m$ matrix:
\[ \mathbf{Y}_t = F_t\, \theta_t + v_t, \qquad v_t \sim \mathcal{N}_m(0,\, V), \]
with $\mathbf{Y}_t = (Y_t^{(1)}, \dots, Y_t^{(m)})^\top$ and $V$ an $m \times m$ (possibly non-diagonal) matrix. Component-wise:
\[ Y_t^{(i)} = \alpha_t^{(i)} + \beta_t^{(i)}\, x_t + v_t^{(i)}, \quad i = 1, \dots, m. \]
\emph{Distributional form.} $\mathbf{Y}_t \mid \theta_t \sim \mathcal{N}_m\!\bigl(F_t\, \theta_t,\, V\bigr)$.

\emph{Parameter counts.} State noise: $m(m+1)$ free entries in $W_\alpha + W_\beta$. Obs noise: $m(m+1)/2$ in $V$. So total $\mathcal{O}(m^2)$ noise parameters --- scales gracefully with $m$ thanks to the Kronecker structure.

\emph{CAPM example.} $m = 4$ assets (Mobil, IBM, Weyer, Citicorp), $x_t = R_{m,t} - R_{f,t}$ shared market excess return. State $\theta_t \in \mathbb{R}^8$ (4 alphas $+$ 4 betas); $W_\alpha, W_\beta$ are $4 \times 4$; $V$ is $4 \times 4$ (cross-stock residual correlation).

trash.title: Example — Nile river
trash.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{EXAMPLE --- Nile river data}}

In LAB 2 we consider a few examples on the use of HMMs with R, using the R package \texttt{depmixS4}.

The following example considers the \emph{Nile river data}, available in R, which provides the measurements of the annual flow of the Nile river in the period 1871--1970. We envisage a change point around the year 1898, when the construction of the first dam in Aswan was started. This suggests to fit an HMM with $K = 2$ states --- so $(S_t)_{t \ge 0}$ is a Markov chain with state space $\mathcal{S} = \{1, 2\}$ --- and to assume a \emph{Gaussian emission distribution} with state-specific parameters:
\[ \begin{aligned} Y_t \mid S_t = 1 &\;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(\mu_1^*, \sigma_1^*), \\ Y_t \mid S_t = 2 &\;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(\mu_2^*, \sigma_2^*), \end{aligned} \]
where the (unknown) parameters are $\theta_1^* = (\mu_1^*, \sigma_1^*)$ and $\theta_2^* = (\mu_2^*, \sigma_2^*)$. We also fix the initial distribution as
\[ \pi \;=\; \bigl(\, \pi_1 = 0, \;\; \pi_2 = 1 \,\bigr). \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{The "equation" of the hidden chain.}} For this 2-state chain, the conditional law of $S_t$ given $S_{t-1} = i$ is the categorical distribution given by row $i$ of $\mathbf{P}$:
\[ S_t \mid S_{t-1} = i \;\sim\; \text{Categorical}\bigl(p_{i,1}, p_{i,2}, \dots, p_{i,K}\bigr), \]
i.e.\ $P(S_t = j \mid S_{t-1} = i) = p_{i,j}$, plus the initial law $S_0 \sim \pi$. This is the "equation" of a Markov chain.





\textbf{\textcolor{red}{MLE of the transition matrix.}} The maximum likelihood estimates of the transition matrix, provided by \texttt{depmixS4}, are
\begin{tabular}{c|cc} $t-1 \backslash t$ & $1$ & $2$ \\ \hline $1$ & $1.00$ & $0.00$ \\ $2$ & $0.04$ & $0.97$ \end{tabular}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{MLE of the emission parameters.}} The MLEs of the parameters $\theta_j^*$ are
\[ \hat\theta_1^* = (\hat\mu_1^*, \hat\sigma_1^*) = (850.57,\; 124.45), \qquad \hat\theta_2^* = (\hat\mu_2^*, \hat\sigma_2^*) = (1097.15,\; 133.75). \]

\emph{Remark.} Reporting the MLEs is not enough. One should also provide the \textbf{standard errors} of the MLEs (possibly approximated by bootstrap techniques), or at least their \emph{asymptotic} standard errors, obtained from the asymptotic properties of MLEs. The computation of the standard errors for the MLEs of the fitted HMM, using the R package \texttt{depmixS4}, is illustrated in Lab 2.

trash.title: Derivation: Filtering
trash.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Deriving $f(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t-1})$ (one line, three rules).}}

\[ f(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t-1}) \;\underbrace{=}_{(1)}\; \int f(\theta_t,\, \theta_{t-1} \mid y_{1:t-1})\, d\theta_{t-1} \;\underbrace{=}_{(2)}\; \int f(\theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1},\, y_{1:t-1})\, f(\theta_{t-1} \mid y_{1:t-1})\, d\theta_{t-1} \;\underbrace{=}_{(3)}\; \int \underbrace{f(\theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1})}_{\text{transition}}\, \underbrace{f(\theta_{t-1} \mid y_{1:t-1})}_{\text{yesterday's posterior}}\, d\theta_{t-1}. \]

\textbf{(1)} \emph{Marginalisation (law of total probability):} introduce $\theta_{t-1}$ by integrating over it.

\textbf{(2)} \emph{Chain rule} $f(A \cap B \mid C) = f(A \mid B,\, C)\, f(B \mid C)$ with $A = \theta_t$, $B = \theta_{t-1}$, $C = y_{1:t-1}$.

\textbf{(3)} \emph{Markov property of the latent process:} given $\theta_{t-1}$, the next state $\theta_t$ doesn't depend on past observations, so $f(\theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1},\, y_{1:t-1}) = f(\theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1})$.

\emph{Interpretation.} Today's predicted state distribution $=$ average (integral) of the transition probabilities from yesterday to today, weighted by yesterday's posterior --- "where you were yesterday."

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{The filtering recursion (Case 2, full).}}
\[ \boxed{\; f(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t}) \;\propto\; \underbrace{f(y_t \mid \theta_t)}_{\text{single new emission}} \;\cdot\; \underbrace{f(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t-1})}_{\substack{\text{predicted prior} \\ \text{(integrate transition} \\ \text{against yesterday's posterior)}}}. \;} \]
\emph{Step pattern.} \textbf{Predict} (transition forward) $\to$ \textbf{update} (Bayes with $y_t$). Repeat at each $t$.

trash.title: Derivation: Prediction
trash.content:
\[ {\; f(y_{t+h} \mid y_{1:t}) \;\underbrace{=}_{\text{Marginalization}}\; \int f(y_{t+h},\, \theta_{t+h} \mid y_{1:t})\, d\theta_{t+h} \;\underbrace{=}_{\text{Bayes on the integrand}}\; \int f(y_{t+h} \mid y_{1:t},\, \theta_{t+h})\, f(\theta_{t+h} \mid y_{1:t})\, d\theta_{t+h} \;=\; \int f(y_{t+h} \mid \theta_{t+h})\, \underbrace{f(\theta_{t+h} \mid y_{1:t})}_{\text{filter + predict}}\, d\theta_{t+h}. \;} \]

 The integration variable must match what's varying in the integrand.

\emph{Reading.} \textbf{KEY:} For each candidate value of the contemporaneous state $\theta_{t+h}$, the emission gives a forecast $f(y_{t+h} \mid \theta_{t+h})$; we average these forecasts, weighted by how plausible each $\theta_{t+h}$ is given the data we have already seen ($f(\theta_{t+h} \mid y_{1:t})$, the predicted-state distribution).
