trash.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{1. MODEL SPECIFICATION}}

Choosing the number $K$ of hidden states is a natural first question. In some applications, $K$ is suggested by knowledge of the domain under study. In other cases, one can try a few different values of $K$ and compare the performance of the resulting models.

trash.title: Example emission matrices
trash.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{2. Parametric case --- Poisson emissions.}} In other cases one may want a parametric emission distribution, so that $Y_t \mid S_t = j \sim p(\,\cdot \mid \theta_j^*)$, $j = 1, \dots, K$. For example, for the earthquakes data (unbounded counts), one could assume
\[ Y_t \mid (S_t = j) \;\sim\; \text{Poisson}(\theta_j^*), \]
that is, at state $j$, $Y_t$ has a Poisson distribution with parameter $\theta_j^*$. Note how the parameter can switch across states!

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Why this fixes the plain-Poisson defects.}} A single Poisson forces (i) mean $=$ variance, (ii) no serial dependence. Letting the rate \emph{switch} with a Markov chain breaks all three:

$\bullet$ \textbf{Different mean and variance per regime.} Within state $j$, both equal $\lambda_j^*$, but across regimes they differ --- a "quiet" state has small mean \emph{and} small variance, an "active" one has large mean \emph{and} large variance.

$\bullet$ \textbf{Autocorrelation.} Sticky regimes ($p_{j,j}$ near $1$) mean neighbouring $Y_t$'s likely share the same rate, so
\[ \text{Cov}(Y_t, Y_{t+h}) \;=\; \text{Cov}(\lambda_{S_t}^*, \lambda_{S_{t+h}}^*) \;>\; 0. \]
No additive $\epsilon$ needed --- the dependence comes from persistence of the hidden chain.

trash.title: Ex.1 Most trivial example of stoch. process
trash.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{MOST TRIVIAL EXAMPLE OF STOCH.\ PROCESS}}

\textbf{IID stochastic processes}
Say $Y_t,\ t \ge 0$ are independent. If, additionally, $Y_t$ have a common distribution (i.i.d.) with $p$:
\[ p_n(y_1,\dots,y_n) = p(y_1)\, p(y_2) \cdots p(y_n) = \prod_{i=1}^n p(y_i). \]

\emph{Example} Independent trials $Y_t \stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim}$ Bernoulli$(p)$.

Transition matrix:
\[ \begin{array}{c|cc} t-1 \backslash t & 0 & 1 \\ \hline 0 & 1-p & p \\ 1 & 1-p & p \end{array} \]


\textbf{ID stochastic processes}
If only indep.\ (not necessarily identically distrib.):
\[ p_n(y_1,\dots,y_n) = p_1(y_1)\, p_2(y_2) \cdots p_n(y_n). \]



Both assume independence: irrealistic for time series

trash.title: Example 2. White noise
trash.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{EXAMPLE 2 — WHITE NOISE}}

A \textbf{white noise} is a process $(Y_t)_{t \ge 1}$ such that the $Y_t$ are iid and:\[ \mathbb{E}[Y_t] = \mu, \qquad \mathrm{Var}(Y_t) = \sigma^2, \qquad \gamma(t, t') = \mathrm{Cov}(Y_t, Y_{t'}) = 0 \ \text{for } t \neq t'. \]

trash.title: Introducing correlation — full dependence
trash.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{INTRODUCING CORRELATION (DEPENDENCE)}}

\textbf{Step 1 — Full dependence (general chain rule).}\[ p_n(y_1, \dots, y_n) = p(y_1)\, p(y_2 \mid y_1)\, p(y_3 \mid y_1, y_2) \cdots p(y_n \mid y_1, \dots, y_{n-1}) = p(y_1) \prod_{t=2}^{n} p(y_t \mid y_1, \dots, y_{t-1}). \]This is fully general — no assumption made. The cost is that each conditional $p(y_t \mid y_1, \dots, y_{t-1})$ depends on the \emph{entire} past, so we have $n-1$ growing-dimension conditionals to specify or estimate. Infeasible in practice.

trash.title: Inference (here the markov chain is observed)
trash.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{INFERENCE FOR MARKOV CHAINS}} \emph{(panel of i.i.d.\ chains)}

\textbf{Setting.} When a Markov chain is used as a statistical model, the transition probabilities $p_{i,j}$ are unknown and must be estimated from data. 

Causality: see if transition probabilities chnage after treatment 
Prediction: infer the transition probabilities to predict future values. 

Two data designs:

$\bullet$ \emph{Single long path:} we observe one trajectory $(Y_0, Y_1, \dots, Y_T)$ for $T$ large; estimate $p_{i,j}$ from time averages.

$\bullet$ \emph{Panel:} we observe $n$ short trajectories $(Y_{k,0}, \dots, Y_{k,T})$, $k = 1, \dots, n$, one per individual. This is the Anderson \& Goodman (1957) setting; we focus on this case. In other words, we have a random sample of markov chains characterized by the same transition matrices! (eg voting preferences across time), aggregated for n individuals.

\textbf{Modelling assumptions:}  M1) homogeneous Markov, M2) trajectories are i.i.d.\ across individuals: no spillovers + Identical distribution (the marginals are all the same, notice this is different from saying the marginals are time invariant (homogeneous)). 

\textit{Caveats one may want to relax:} higher-order Markov (memory $r > 1$); non-homogeneity ($\mathbf{P}_t$ depends on $t$); individual-specific transition matrices (heterogeneity).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{HIDDEN MARKOV MODELS (HMM)}}


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Toy 3-regime Gaussian HMM.}} A simple example with three regimes is\[ Y_t = \begin{cases} \mu_1 + e_t & \text{if } S_t = 1, \\ \mu_2 + e_t & \text{if } S_t = 2, \\ \mu_3 + e_t & \text{if } S_t = 3, \end{cases} \qquad e_t \stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2). \]More compactly, $Y_t = \mu_{S_t} + e_t$.

$\bullet$ the \textbf{emission distributions} $\{p(y \mid s) : s \in \mathcal{S}\}$, one per state
